Lens & Mirror Sign Conventions

  1. Converging (convex lens / concave mirror): f is positive.
  2. Diverging (concave lens / convex mirror): f is negative.
  3. Real image: di is positive; can be projected onto a screen.
  4. Virtual image: di is negative; cannot be projected onto a screen.
  5. Upright image: magnification m is positive.
  6. Inverted image: magnification m is negative.
  7. A converging lens/mirror forms a real image only when the object is beyond the focal point (do > f).
  8. A diverging lens/mirror ALWAYS forms a virtual, upright, reduced image, regardless of object distance.

Exam Day Checklist

  • Write down every given value with its units before starting a calculation.
  • Choose the correct kinematic equation based on which variable is missing.
  • Draw a free-body diagram before applying Newton's Second Law.
  • For circular motion, remember the centripetal force is supplied by a real force — identify which one.
  • Check whether a collision is elastic or inelastic before assuming kinetic energy is conserved.
  • In circuits, identify series vs. parallel sections before computing total resistance.
  • Use the right-hand rule carefully for magnetic field and force direction problems.
  • For optics, determine real/virtual and upright/inverted using sign conventions, not guesswork.
  • Track units all the way through a calculation — mismatched units signal an error.
  • Double-check sig figs and rounding only in the final answer, not intermediate steps.
memoryHtml:
Quick ways to lock in the facts you keep forgetting. Read the big trick, then the small note tells you what it unlocks. Say them out loud — silly is memorable.

Kinematics

Same sign, speeding; opposite, slowing
If velocity and acceleration have the same sign, the object speeds up. Opposite signs mean it's slowing down — direction alone doesn't tell you.
No time? No place? Pick the matching equation
Each kinematic equation is missing exactly one variable — vf=vi+at skips Δx, Δx=vit+½at² skips vf, vf²=vi²+2aΔx skips t. Match what's missing to what you don't have.
Top of the toss, still falling
At the peak of a thrown ball's path, velocity is zero but acceleration is still −g. Zero velocity does NOT mean zero acceleration.
Sideways and downways don't talk
In projectile motion, horizontal and vertical motions are totally independent — horizontal velocity never changes, vertical acceleration is always −g.

Newton's Laws & Forces

Third law pairs never meet on one object
Action-reaction forces act on two DIFFERENT objects, so they can never cancel each other out on the same free-body diagram.
Mass is yours everywhere, weight isn't
Mass (kg) never changes with location. Weight (N) = mg changes wherever gravity changes — that's why you'd weigh less on the Moon but have the same mass.
Friction depends on push-down, not push-across
Friction force = μ×FN depends on how hard surfaces press together (normal force), never on the contact area.
Constant velocity means balanced, not motionless
Zero NET force means constant velocity, which includes rest — but also includes cruising at any constant speed in a straight line.

Momentum & Energy

Momentum always survives, energy sometimes doesn't
Momentum is conserved in EVERY collision. Kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions — inelastic ones lose some to heat/sound.
Perpendicular force does nothing
If a force is at 90° to the displacement, W = Fd cos90° = 0. Carrying a bag level, or moving in a circle — no work is done.
Double the speed, quadruple the energy
KE = ½mv² depends on velocity SQUARED — doubling speed doesn't double kinetic energy, it quadruples it.
Longer time, softer hit
Airbags and padding stretch out the time of impact for the same impulse (Δp), which lowers the force (J=FΔt) and reduces injury.

Circular Motion & Gravity

Centripetal isn't its own force — it's a job title
"Centripetal force" just describes the inward net force — it's actually supplied by tension, gravity, friction, or normal force, never a separate force type.
There's no real push outward
The "flung outward" feeling in a turning car is just your own inertia resisting the turn — there is no real outward (centrifugal) force acting on you.
Double the distance, quarter the pull
Gravity (and Coulomb's law) follow inverse-square laws — doubling distance cuts the force to 1/4, not 1/2.
Farther out, slower orbit
A satellite in a bigger orbit moves slower (v=√(GM/r)) — and its own mass doesn't matter at all.

Waves & Sound

The medium sets the speed limit
Wave speed (v=fλ) depends on the medium only. Change the frequency and wavelength adjusts to compensate — speed doesn't budge.
No stuff, no sound
Sound needs particles to compress and rarefy, so it can't cross a vacuum. Light doesn't need a medium — that's the key difference.
Toward you = squeezed = higher pitch
Doppler effect: a source moving toward you compresses wavefronts (higher perceived pitch); moving away stretches them (lower pitch) — the source's own frequency never changes.

Electricity

Series shares current, parallel shares voltage
In series, the SAME current flows through everything. In parallel, the SAME voltage sits across every branch. Never mix these up.
Parallel resistance always shrinks
Adding a parallel branch gives current another path, so total resistance always drops BELOW the smallest single resistor.
Electric force swings both ways
Unlike gravity (always attractive), Coulomb force can push or pull — like charges repel, opposite charges attract.

Magnetism

Parallel to the field means zero force
F=qvB sinθ — if a charge moves parallel to B (θ=0°), sinθ=0 and the magnetic force vanishes.
No monopoles, ever
You can never isolate just a north or south pole — cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with both poles.
No change, no current
Electromagnetic induction needs a CHANGING magnetic flux — a stationary loop sitting in a constant field induces absolutely nothing.

Optics

Denser bends it in, thinner bends it out
Light bends TOWARD the normal entering a denser (higher-n) medium, and AWAY from the normal entering a thinner one.
Convex mirrors never lie big
A convex (diverging) mirror always makes a virtual, upright, SMALLER image — no exceptions, regardless of object distance.
Real flips it, virtual doesn't
Real images (projectable on a screen) from a single lens or mirror are always inverted. Virtual images are always upright.

Modern Physics

Intensity = more electrons, frequency = stronger electrons
In the photoelectric effect, brighter light ejects MORE electrons; higher-frequency light ejects FASTER (higher-KE) electrons — two different jobs.
Alpha's heavy and slow, gamma's light and fast
Alpha particles are big, stopped by paper, but very ionizing. Gamma rays are pure energy, pass through almost anything, but ionize the least.
Half of what's left, every half-life
Half-life always removes half of whatever remains — it's exponential decay, never a constant number of atoms per unit time.

units.name: Measurement, Vectors & Motion Basics

concepts.intro: Test #1 starts with the math every later problem uses: rearranging formulas, right-triangle trig, and unit conversions.
b: Solve for the unknown with symbols first, then substitute numbers with their units: $d = \tfrac12at^2$ becomes $t = \sqrt{2d/a}$.
Right-triangle trig (SOH-CAH-TOA): $\sinθ = opp/hyp$, $\cosθ = adj/hyp$, $\tanθ = opp/adj$; the Pythagorean theorem gives $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Slope of a straight-line graph = rise ÷ run, with units (m ÷ s = m/s).
Convert units by multiplying by fractions equal to 1: $72 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 20 m/s$ (divide km/h by 3.6).
Keep units through every step; if the final unit is wrong, the setup is wrong.

concepts.intro: Physics is built on measurement, and every measurement is a number plus a unit. Drop the unit and the answer is incomplete.
b: The SI system has seven base units; the three used most in mechanics are the meter (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, and the second (s) for time.
The other base units are the ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), and candela (cd).
Derived units are combinations of base units: speed is m/s, and force is the newton, $N = kg·m/s^2$.
Quantities that are added or subtracted must have the same units, and a final answer must carry the correct unit.
Volume: $1 cm^3 = 1 mL$ and $1 m^3 = 1000 L$; for water, $1 mL = 1 g$.

concepts.intro: Prefixes scale a unit by powers of 10, which is what makes the metric system a decimal system.
b: To convert, replace the prefix with its power of 10: $3.5 km = 3.5 × 10^3 m$ and $1 MW = 10^6 W$.
Handy sizes: an adult is about 1.75 m tall, a classroom is about 10 m long, a physics textbook has a mass near 1 kg, and a high school student is about 60 kg.

concepts.intro: Scientific notation keeps very large and very small numbers manageable and makes calculations mechanical.
b: Write a number as $M × 10^n$ with $1 ≤ M < 10$ and n an integer.
Move the decimal point until one nonzero digit is left of it; the number of places moved is the exponent (positive for big numbers, negative for small ones).
To add or subtract, first rewrite both terms with the same power of 10, then combine the M values: $4.1×10^{-6} − 0.3×10^{-6} = 3.8×10^{-6}$.
To multiply, multiply the M values and add the exponents; to divide, divide the M values and subtract the exponents. Multiply and divide the units too.
Order of magnitude is the power of 10 closest to the value: $1284 kg = 1.284×10^3$ kg is order $10^3$, but $8756 kg = 8.756×10^3$ kg is closer to $10^4$.
Estimate with benchmarks: one building story ≈ 3 m, so a 30-story building ≈ 90 m ≈ $10^2$ m; a football field ≈ 100 m = 1000 dm.
Small benchmarks: a little finger is about 1 cm = 0.01 m wide; a pencil is about 5 g = $5.0 × 10^{-3}$ kg; an adult is about 70 kg.

concepts.intro: No measurement is exact, so physicists track how precise and how accurate it is.
b: Precision is the smallest decimal place in a measurement; the instrument's scale markings set it, and one estimated digit is read beyond the smallest marked interval.
Accuracy is closeness to the accepted value. Absolute error = |measured − accepted|; percent error = |measured − accepted| / accepted × 100%.
Systematic errors push every reading the same way (fix by calibrating); random errors scatter readings high and low (reduce by averaging many trials).
Significant figures: nonzero digits, zeros between digits, and trailing zeros after a decimal point count; leading zeros do not.
A calculated answer can be no more precise than the least precise measurement used.

concepts.l: Lab skills: can capacity & distance vs. displacement
concepts.intro: Labs 1.1 and 1.2 practice measuring carefully and telling a path from a straight-line change in position.
b: Lab 1.1: a can is a cylinder, so its capacity is $V = πr^2h$. Measure the diameter and halve it for r; using the diameter by mistake makes V four times too big.
$1 cm^3 = 1 mL$, so a can 6.6 cm across and 12.2 cm tall holds about $π(3.3)^2(12.2) ≈ 417 mL$.
Record every measurement with its unit and the instrument's precision, and compare with the accepted value using percent error.
Lab 1.2: walking a path, distance is the total length walked; displacement is the straight line from start to finish plus its direction.
Halfway around a 30 m × 40 m rectangle (to the opposite corner), the distance is 70 m but the displacement is 50 m.

concepts.intro: Some quantities need only a size; others also need a direction.
b: A scalar has magnitude only: mass, length, time, distance, speed, density, energy, temperature.
A vector has magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, electric and magnetic field strength.
A vector is drawn as an arrow: its length shows the magnitude (never negative) and the tail-to-head direction shows the direction.
In print a vector is bold; handwritten, an arrow goes over the letter.
Concurrent vectors act on the same point at the same time.

concepts.intro: The sum of vectors is called the resultant, and it can be found by drawing.
b: Head-to-tail: place the second vector's tail at the first one's head; the resultant runs from the first tail to the last head.
Parallelogram: draw both vectors from a common tail and complete the parallelogram; the diagonal from that tail is the resultant.
Order does not matter: $A + B = B + A$. In one dimension, just add with signs, so opposite directions partly cancel.
To subtract, add the negative: $A − B = A + (−B)$, where $−B$ has the same length but points the opposite way.
Multiplying by a positive scalar changes only the length; a negative scalar also reverses the direction.
The resultant of two vectors is largest ($A + B$) at 0° between them, smallest ($|A − B|$) at 180°, and shrinks steadily as the angle grows from 0° to 180°.

concepts.intro: Tip-to-tail diagrams are drawn to scale, so the length of each arrow stands for its magnitude.
b: Choose a scale and keep it for every vector: if 15 mm represents 30 m/s, then 1 mm = 2 m/s and 20 m/s is drawn 10 mm long.
Two vectors A and B combine to anything from $|A − B|$ (opposite directions, 180°) to $A + B$ (same direction, 0°): 3 m and 4 m give 1 m to 7 m, and 5 m at 90°.
As the angle between two vectors grows from 0° to 180°, their resultant shrinks steadily from the sum to the difference.
Relative velocity: add velocities as vectors. Walking forward at 4.0 m/s in a bus moving at 2.0 m/s gives 6.0 m/s relative to the street; walking toward the back gives 2.0 m/s the other way.
Measure the resultant's length and angle on the drawing, then convert back with the scale.

concepts.intro: When two vectors are at right angles, the resultant comes straight from a right triangle.
b: Magnitude: $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$.
Direction: $\tanθ = B/A$, where θ is measured from vector A toward B.
Example: 5 m east then 2 m north gives $R = \sqrt{29} ≈ 5.4$ m at about 22° north of east.
Boat aimed straight across a river: 10 km/h in still water with a 4 km/h current gives $\sqrt{10^2 + 4^2} ≈ 10.8$ km/h, angled downstream.
The equilibrant has the same magnitude as the resultant but points the opposite way; adding it makes the net vector zero.

concepts.intro: Any vector can be replaced by two perpendicular components, which turns angled problems into simple x and y arithmetic.
b: With θ measured from the horizontal: $A_x = A\cosθ$ and $A_y = A\sinθ$.
Example: 60. N at 30° above horizontal gives $A_x = 60\cos30° ≈ 52$ N and $A_y = 60\sin30° = 30$ N.
To add vectors analytically: resolve each into x and y components, add all the x parts and all the y parts separately, then combine them with the Pythagorean theorem.
As θ from the horizontal grows toward 90°, the horizontal component shrinks and the vertical one grows.
On an incline of angle θ, the weight's component parallel to the slope is $F_g\sinθ$.

concepts.intro: These are the scalar ways to describe motion: how far, and how fast.
b: Distance is the total length of the path traveled; it is a scalar, never negative, measured in meters.
Average speed is total distance divided by total time: $v = d/t$, in m/s. Include any time spent stopped.
Instantaneous speed is how fast you are moving at one moment, like a speedometer reading.
Speed has no direction, so a car going around a circular track at 20 m/s has constant speed even though its direction keeps changing.

concepts.intro: These are the vector versions: they track where you ended up relative to where you started.
b: Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish plus the direction, for example 5 m south.
In one dimension displacement is positive or negative depending on direction; it can be zero after a round trip, and its magnitude never exceeds the distance traveled.
Average velocity is displacement divided by time: $\bar v = Δd/Δt$, in m/s, in the direction of the displacement.
Instantaneous velocity is speed and direction at one instant (a speedometer plus a compass).
By convention forward, right, and up are positive; backward, left, and down are negative.
Constant velocity requires both constant speed and constant direction.

concepts.intro: Uniform motion means constant velocity: the same speed in the same direction for the whole time interval.
b: On a velocity–time graph, constant velocity is a horizontal straight line (parallel to the time axis).
On a distance–time (or position–time) graph, constant velocity is a straight sloped line.
The slope of a d–t graph is the velocity: its size is the speed and its sign is the direction (positive slope = positive direction, negative slope = negative direction).
A horizontal line on a d–t graph means the object is not moving.
The area under a v–t graph is the distance traveled: for constant velocity, $d = vt$ is just the rectangle's area.

concepts.intro: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. It is a vector, measured in $m/s^2$.
b: Average acceleration: $a = Δv/Δt = (v_f − v_i)/t$.
Velocity can change in speed, in direction, or both, so a car rounding a curve at constant speed is still accelerating.
Negative acceleration just points in the negative direction. Deceleration means the acceleration is opposite to the velocity, so the object slows down.
An object with negative velocity and negative acceleration is speeding up (in the negative direction).
Zero acceleration means constant velocity; the object may be at rest or moving.
For constant acceleration only: $v_f = v_0 + at$, $d = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$, $v_f^2 = v_0^2 + 2ad$, and $d = \tfrac12(v_0 + v_f)t$.

concepts.intro: When velocity changes, the position–time graph curves, and the velocity–time graph carries the acceleration.
b: Nonuniform motion shows up as a curved line on a d–t graph.
Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent line at one point on the d–t curve; average velocity is the slope of the straight line joining the start and end points.
Where the tangent is horizontal (slope zero) the object is momentarily at rest; where the slope changes sign, it has turned around.
The slope of a v–t graph is the acceleration: positive slope means the velocity is increasing, negative slope means it is decreasing, and a flat line means zero acceleration.
The area under a v–t graph is still the distance traveled, even when the line slopes (use triangles and rectangles).
$v = v_0 + at$ has the same form as $y = mx + b$: on a v–t graph the slope is $a$ and the vertical intercept is $v_0$.

concepts.intro: Vectors can also be multiplied by each other in two ways, which matter later for work and magnetism.
b: Dot product: $A·B = AB\cosθ$ is a scalar, used for work and power; it is zero for perpendicular vectors.
Cross product: $A×B$ is a vector with magnitude $AB\sinθ$, perpendicular to both, found with the right-hand rule; it is zero for parallel vectors.
Order matters for the cross product: $B×A = −(A×B)$.

traps: Writing a numeric answer with no unit, or the wrong unit; a correct number can still lose half the credit.
Adding vector magnitudes directly (3 N + 4 N = 7 N) when the vectors are not in the same direction.
Using cos for the vertical component or sin for the horizontal when θ is measured from the horizontal.
Treating distance and displacement as the same thing; a round trip has zero displacement but nonzero distance.
Adding numbers in scientific notation without first matching the powers of 10.
Calling every negative acceleration 'slowing down': an object only slows when its acceleration points opposite to its velocity.
Averaging two speeds for a round trip (60 and 75 km/h → 67.5): average speed is always total distance ÷ total time (300 km ÷ 4.5 h ≈ 67 km/h).
Using the diameter instead of the radius in $V = πr^2h$.
fms: SOH-CAH-TOA: $\sinθ = opp/hyp$, $\cosθ = adj/hyp$, $\tanθ = opp/adj$; km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s.
$M × 10^n$ with $1 ≤ M < 10$; multiply → add exponents, divide → subtract exponents.
Percent error $= |measured − accepted| / accepted × 100\%$.
$R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$ for perpendicular vectors; $|A − B| ≤ R ≤ A + B$ in general.
$A_x = A\cosθ$, $A_y = A\sinθ$ (θ from the horizontal).
Average speed $v = d/t$ (scalar); average velocity $\bar v = Δd/Δt$ (vector).
$a = Δv/Δt$; constant a: $v_f = v_0 + at$, $d = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$, $v_f^2 = v_0^2 + 2ad$.
Slope of d–t = velocity; slope of v–t = acceleration; area under v–t = distance.
Cylinder (can): $V = πr^2h$; $1 cm^3 = 1 mL$. Resultant of A and B: $|A − B| ≤ R ≤ A + B$.

units.name: Kinematics

concepts.intro: Kinematics begins by separating how far you traveled from how far you ended up from the start.
b: Distance is total path length; it is a scalar and never negative.
Displacement is the straight-line change in position, $Δx = x_f − x_i$; a vector with a sign in 1D.
A round trip has zero displacement but nonzero distance.
Choose a positive direction first; every sign in the problem is relative to that choice.
SI unit for both is the meter.

concepts.intro: The rate words split the same way: one keeps direction, one does not.
b: Average speed = total distance / total time (scalar, ≥ 0).
Average velocity = displacement / time, $v_{avg} = Δx/Δt$ (vector).
Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the x–t graph at that instant.
Constant velocity means unchanging speed AND direction.
Unit: m/s.

concepts.intro: Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes; graphs make the relationships visible.
b: $a_{avg} = Δv/Δt$, units $m/s^2$.
Positive acceleration means velocity is becoming more positive — not necessarily speeding up.
Speeding up: a and v point the same way. Slowing down: opposite ways.
Slope of x–t is velocity; slope of v–t is acceleration; area under v–t is displacement.
A straight line on a v–t graph means constant acceleration.

concepts.intro: Four equations link displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time when acceleration is constant.
b: $v = v_0 + at$
Pick the equation missing the quantity you neither know nor want.

concepts.intro: Near Earth's surface, gravity alone gives every object the same downward acceleration.
b: g ≈ $9.8 m/s^2$ downward (air resistance neglected).
At the top of a vertical toss, velocity is zero but acceleration is still g downward.
Time up equals time down for a symmetric path; return speed equals launch speed.
Substitute a = −g (with up positive) into the kinematic equations.
A dropped object and one thrown horizontally from the same height fall for the same time.
Aristotle taught that heavier objects fall faster. Galileo showed that, without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration.
In a vacuum tube a coin and a feather land together; on the Moon, Apollo 15's hammer and feather hit the ground at the same time.
Near Earth's surface $g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2$, always directed downward; with up as positive, use $a = −g$.
Dropped from rest: $v_f = gt$, $d = \tfrac12gt^2$, $v_f^2 = 2gd$.
Thrown straight up: the velocity decreases by 9.8 m/s every second, is zero at the top, and the acceleration is still $g$ downward the whole time.
Reaction time from a dropped ruler: $t = \sqrt{2d/g}$, where d is how far it fell before you caught it (about 0.2 s for most people).

concepts.intro: Two-dimensional launches are solved by treating horizontal and vertical motion as independent, sharing only time.
b: Horizontal: $a_x = 0$, so $v_x = v_0 \cosθ$ stays constant.
Vertical: $a_y = −g$, so the y-motion is free fall with $v_{0y} = v_0 \sinθ$.
Time to the peak = $v_{0y}/g$; total flight time on level ground = twice that.
Range on level ground $R = v_0^2 \sin(2θ)/g$, maximized at 45°; 30° and 60° tie.
Impact speed = $\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$.

traps: Using the kinematic equations when acceleration is not constant.
Thinking a projectile at its peak has a = 0 — it is still g downward.
Using the full launch speed as the horizontal speed instead of $v_0 \cosθ$.
Switching sign conventions partway through a problem.
Saying the acceleration is zero at the top of a vertical toss; the velocity is zero there, but the acceleration is still g downward.
Assuming heavier objects fall faster; without air resistance every object falls with the same acceleration.
fms: Same launch height → same fall time, whatever the horizontal speed.
If time is the missing quantity, use $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2aΔx$.
Slope of x–t = velocity; slope of v–t = acceleration; area under v–t = displacement.
Split the projectile into x and y, solve each, reunite through the shared time t.
Free fall from rest: $v = gt$, $d = \tfrac12gt^2$, $t = \sqrt{2d/g}$, $g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2$.

units.name: Newton's Laws & Dynamics

concepts.intro: A force is a push or pull; a free-body diagram isolates one object and shows every force on it.
b: Force is a vector in newtons $(1 N = 1 kg·m/s^2)$.
Draw the object as a dot; draw each force as an arrow from the dot.
Common forces: weight (down), normal (perpendicular to surface), tension, friction, applied.
Include only forces acting ON the object, not forces it exerts on others.
Choose axes along and perpendicular to the acceleration.

concepts.intro: An object keeps doing what it is doing unless a net force acts.
b: Zero net force means zero acceleration — at rest or constant velocity (equilibrium).
Inertia is resistance to a change in motion; mass measures it.
There is no 'force of motion' keeping a sliding object going; it coasts until friction stops it.
Equilibrium: $ΣF_x = 0$ and $ΣF_y = 0$.
A frame moving at constant velocity is also an inertial frame.

concepts.intro: Net force sets acceleration, scaled by mass.
b: $ΣF =$ ma, applied per axis: $ΣF_x = ma_x, ΣF_y = ma_y$.
Acceleration points in the direction of the net force.
Double the net force → double the acceleration; double the mass → half the acceleration.
Weight W = mg is a force, distinct from mass.
Keep units consistent: kg, $m/s^2, N$.

concepts.intro: Forces come in equal, opposite pairs acting on two different objects.
b: If A pushes B, B pushes A equally hard in the opposite direction.
The two forces in a pair never act on the same object, so they never cancel on one free-body diagram.
Action–reaction pairs are the same type of force.
Rocket propulsion: engine pushes gas back, gas pushes rocket forward.
The forces are equal even when the two masses differ greatly.

concepts.intro: Friction opposes sliding; inclined planes require resolving weight into components.
b: Kinetic friction: $f_k = μ_k N$, opposing motion, roughly constant.
Static friction: $f_s$ ≤ $μ_s N$ — it adjusts up to a maximum, then the object breaks free.
$μ_s$ is usually greater than $μ_k$, so starting to slide takes more force than continuing.
On an incline of angle $θ$: N = mg $\cosθ$, and the gravity component along the incline is mg $\sinθ$.
Friction depends on the normal force and surfaces, not on contact area.

traps: Treating action–reaction pairs as forces that cancel — they act on different objects.
Setting $f_s = μ_s N$ when the object is not on the verge of slipping (that is only the maximum).
Assuming the normal force always equals mg — it changes on inclines and in elevators.
Forgetting to resolve weight into components on an inclined plane.
fms: $a = ΣF / m$ — net force first, then divide by mass.
Normal force is whatever it must be to prevent sinking into the surface; solve for it.
Static friction is a range (≤); kinetic friction is a value (=).
On an incline: $\sinθ$ pulls it down the slope, $\cosθ$ presses it into the slope.

units.name: Circular Motion & Gravitation

concepts.intro: Moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because the direction changes.
b: Velocity is tangent to the circle and constantly changes direction.
Centripetal acceleration points to the center: $a_c = v^2 / r$.
Period T is the time for one revolution; $v = 2πr / T$.
Constant speed means no tangential acceleration — only centripetal.
Also $a_c = 4π^2 r / T^2$.

concepts.intro: Some real force must supply the inward pull that bends the path into a circle.
b: $ΣF$ toward the center = $m v^2 / r$.
'Centripetal force' is a role played by tension, gravity, friction, or the normal force.
Car on a flat curve: static friction is the centripetal force.
Vertical circle at the top: mg $+ T = m v^2 / r$.
There is no outward 'centrifugal force' in a ground frame — that feeling is inertia.

concepts.intro: Every mass attracts every other mass along the line joining them.
b: r is the center-to-center distance, not the surface separation.
Inverse-square: triple the distance → one-ninth the force.
The force on each mass is equal in magnitude, even if the masses differ.
Surface gravity: $g = G M / R^2$.

concepts.intro: A satellite is in continuous free fall; gravity is its centripetal force.
b: $G M m / r^2 = m v^2 / r$, so orbital speed v = sqrt(G M / r).
Larger orbits are slower.
Astronauts feel weightless because they fall with the station, not because gravity is absent.
Kepler's third law: $T^2$ is proportional to $r^3$ for one central body.
A geostationary orbit has a 24-hour period and one specific radius.

concepts.intro: The field g gives the gravitational force per kilogram at a point in space.
b: g = F/m, units N/kg (numerically equal to $m/s^2$).
Weight = mg depends on local g, so it differs on the Moon or at altitude.
Mass is invariant; weight is not.
Field lines point toward the mass; closer spacing means a stronger field.
g decreases with altitude as $1/r^2$ from Earth's center.

traps: Adding an outward centrifugal force to a free-body diagram in a ground frame.
Using surface-to-surface distance instead of center-to-center in $F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2$.
Claiming there is no gravity in orbit — it is nearly as strong as at the surface.
Forgetting that at the top of a vertical circle gravity helps supply the centripetal force.
fms: Centripetal acceleration always points to the center; centrifugal force is not real here.
Inverse-square: distance ×3 → force ÷9.
An orbit is falling and missing the ground; farther orbits are slower.
g has two identical faces: $9.8 m/s^2$ and 9.8 N/kg.

units.name: Rotational Motion & Torque

concepts.intro: Rotation has its own kinematics that mirror straight-line motion.
b: Angular displacement $θ$ (radians), angular velocity $ω = Δθ/Δt (rad/s)$, angular acceleration $α (rad/s^2)$.
Link to linear motion: $s = r θ, v = r ω, a_t = r α$.
The rotational kinematic equations look exactly like the linear ones with $x→θ, v→ω, a→α$.
One revolution = $2π$ radians = 360°.
All points on a rigid rotating body share $ω$ and $α$ but have different linear speeds.

concepts.intro: Torque is the rotational analog of force — the tendency of a force to cause rotation.
b: τ = $r F \sinθ =$ (lever arm) × (force), units N·m.
The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of the force.
A force directed through the axis produces zero torque.
Torque has a sign — counterclockwise is conventionally positive.
More distance from the pivot gives more torque for the same force.

concepts.intro: A balanced object has no net force and no net torque.
b: $Στ = 0$ and $ΣF = 0$ for static equilibrium.
You may take torques about any point — pick one that removes an unknown force.
Balance beam or seesaw: $m_1 g d_1 = m_2 g d_2$.
The weight of a uniform beam acts at its center.
Two equilibrium conditions let you solve for two unknown support forces.

concepts.intro: Moment of inertia is rotational mass — resistance to a change in spin.
b: I depends on mass AND how far that mass sits from the axis (I is proportional to $r^2$).
Point mass: $I = m r^2$. Hoop: $I = M R^2$. Solid disk: $I = 0.5 M R^2$. Solid sphere: $I = 0.4 M R^2$.
Rotational Newton's second law: $Στ = I α$.
Mass far from the axis contributes much more than mass near it.
A figure skater pulling arms in lowers I.

concepts.intro: Spinning objects store kinetic energy and carry angular momentum that is conserved.
b: Rotational KE = $0.5 I ω^2$; a rolling object has $0.5 m v^2 + 0.5 I ω^2$.
Angular momentum $L = I ω$, units $kg·m^2/s$.
With no external torque, L is conserved: $I_1 ω_1 = I_2 ω_2$.
A skater speeds up when arms are pulled in because I drops and L is fixed.
A rolling object accelerates down a ramp slower than a frictionless sliding one.

traps: Using the full distance to the force instead of the perpendicular lever arm in τ = $r F \sinθ$.
Treating moment of inertia as if it depended only on mass, not its distribution.
Forgetting rotational kinetic energy when analyzing a rolling (not sliding) object.
Assuming every point on a rotating disk has the same linear speed.
fms: Torque = force × perpendicular distance to the pivot; through the pivot means no torque.
$Στ = I α$ is just F = ma in rotational form.
Pull mass inward → I down → $ω$ up (angular momentum conserved).
Rolling race: smaller $I/(MR^2)$ wins — sphere beats disk beats hoop.

units.name: Momentum & Energy

concepts.intro: Work is energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement.
b: $W = F d \cosθ$, where $θ$ is the angle between force and displacement.
A force perpendicular to the motion (normal, centripetal) does zero work.
Work is a scalar in joules (1 J = 1 N·m).
Negative work (friction, $θ$ > 90°) removes energy from the object.
On a force-vs-position graph, work is the area under the curve.

concepts.l: Kinetic energy and the work–energy theorem
concepts.intro: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
b: KE = $0.5 m v^2$, always ≥ 0, scalar, in joules.
Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.
Positive net work speeds an object up; negative net work slows it down.
Often faster than kinematics for finding a final speed.

concepts.intro: Stored energy plus kinetic energy is constant when only conservative forces act.
b: Gravitational PE near Earth: PE = mgh, from a chosen reference height.
Elastic PE in an ideal spring: PE = $0.5 k x^2$.
$KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f$ with no friction or drag.
With friction: $KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f +$ energy lost to heat.
Choose two points and write the energy equation — the path between them does not matter.

concepts.intro: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy.
b: $P = W/t = ΔE/Δt$, units watts (1 W = 1 J/s).
Also P = F v for a force pushing an object at speed v.
Same job done faster needs more power, not more work.
1 horsepower ≈ 746 W.
A kilowatt-hour is energy: 1 kW $× 1 h = 3.6 × 10^6 J$.

concepts.intro: Momentum is mass in motion; impulse is the change a net force produces over time.
b: p = m v, a vector in kg·m/s.
Impulse $J = F_{avg} Δt = Δp$, units N·s.
On a force–time graph, impulse is the area under the curve.
Extending the contact time (airbags, bending knees) lowers the peak force for the same $Δp$.
Momentum is not the same as kinetic energy.

concepts.intro: With no external net force, total momentum is unchanged; collisions differ in what happens to kinetic energy.
b: $Σp_{before} = Σp_{after}$ for an isolated system, applied per axis.
Elastic: kinetic energy is also conserved.
Inelastic: some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound, or deformation.
Perfectly inelastic: objects stick together — $m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = (m_1 + m_2) v_f$.
Explosion or recoil from rest: the fragments' momenta must sum to zero.

traps: Using conservation of kinetic energy in an inelastic collision — only momentum is conserved there.
Using mgh with h as the distance along an incline instead of the vertical height.
Counting energy 'lost' to friction as destroyed — it becomes thermal energy.
Confusing impulse (N·s) with force (N), or momentum with kinetic energy.
fms: Perpendicular force → zero work (normal force, centripetal force).
No time given but need a final speed? Use $W_{net} = ΔKE$.
Momentum is always conserved in a collision; kinetic energy only if it is elastic.
Longer collision time → smaller force (why crumple zones work).

units.name: Electricity

concepts.intro: Electric charge comes in two signs and exerts forces described by an inverse-square law.
b: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Charge is quantized in units of e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C.
Charge is conserved; objects charge by moving electrons, not by creating charge.
Coulomb's law: $F = k q_1 q_2 / r^2$, with $k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2$.
Conductors let charge move freely; insulators hold it in place.
Same inverse-square form as gravity, but far stronger and able to attract or repel.

concepts.intro: The field E gives the force per unit charge a small test charge would feel.
b: E = F/q, units N/C (or V/m); it is a vector.
Point charge: $E = k Q / r^2$, pointing away from + and toward −.
Field lines leave + charges, enter − charges, and never cross.
Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, E = 0.
A uniform field exists between parallel charged plates.

concepts.intro: Voltage drives charge through a circuit; current is the resulting flow rate.
b: Potential difference (voltage) is energy per unit charge, in volts (J/C).
Current $I = Δq / Δt$, in amperes (C/s); conventional current is the direction positive charge would move.
A battery's EMF maintains the potential difference that pushes current.
Power delivered: $P = I V = I^2 R = V^2 / R$, in watts.
Electrons drift slowly, but the electrical signal propagates near light speed.

concepts.intro: For many materials, current is proportional to voltage.
b: Ohm's law: V = I R, resistance R in ohms.
Resistance rises with length, falls with cross-sectional area, and depends on material and temperature.
An ohmic device has a straight-line I–V graph through the origin.
Resistors convert electrical energy to heat.
Ideal ammeter: zero resistance, in series. Ideal voltmeter: infinite resistance, in parallel.

concepts.intro: How components are wired sets how voltage, current, and resistance distribute.
b: Series: one path. Same current everywhere; voltages add; $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 +$ ... (increases).
Parallel: multiple paths. Same voltage across each branch; currents add; $1/R_{total} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 +$ ... (decreases).
Adding a parallel resistor lowers total resistance and raises total current from the battery.
A break in a series circuit stops all current; a break in one parallel branch leaves the others working.
At a junction, current in equals current out.

traps: Saying charge is 'created' by rubbing — it is only transferred; total charge is conserved.
Adding parallel resistances directly instead of using the reciprocal rule.
Assuming adding resistors always increases total resistance — in parallel it decreases.
Swapping the ideal ammeter (0 ohm, series) and voltmeter (infinite ohm, parallel) placements.
fms: Series adds resistance; parallel gives less than the smallest branch.
Same current in series; same voltage in parallel.
V = I R, and power has three faces: IV, $I^{2R}, V^2/R$.
Field lines: out of positive, into negative, never crossing.

units.name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism

concepts.intro: Moving charges create magnetic fields and feel forces in them.
b: Field lines run from N to S outside a magnet; isolated poles have never been found.
A current-carrying wire makes a circular magnetic field (right-hand rule: thumb = current, fingers curl = field).
Force on a moving charge: $F = q v B \sinθ$, perpendicular to both v and B.
A charge moving parallel to B feels no force; the force is maximum when v is perpendicular to B.
The magnetic force does no work — it changes direction, not speed, giving circular paths.

concepts.intro: A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces a voltage.
b: Magnetic flux Φ = $B A \cosθ$ through a loop.
Faraday's law: induced EMF = $−ΔΦ/Δt$ — faster flux change means larger EMF.
Flux can change by varying B, the loop area, or the loop's orientation.
Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that produced it (energy conservation).
Basis of generators, transformers, microphones, and induction cooktops.

concepts.intro: The motor force and induction are two sides of the same electromagnetic coin.
b: Motor: current in a field feels a torque → rotation (electrical to mechanical).
Generator: rotating a coil in a field changes flux → induced AC EMF (mechanical to electrical).
Transformer: AC in a primary coil induces AC in a secondary; $V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p$.
A step-up transformer raises voltage and lowers current (ideal: power in = power out).
High-voltage transmission reduces $I^2 R$ losses in power lines.

concepts.intro: A consistent hand convention predicts the direction of magnetic forces and fields.
b: For a moving positive charge: point fingers along v, curl toward B, thumb gives F (reverse for negative charge).
A charged particle entering a uniform field perpendicular to B moves in a circle.
Radius of that circle: r = m v / (q B) — faster or heavier particles curve less.
Parallel currents attract; antiparallel currents repel.
A velocity selector balances electric and magnetic forces: qE = qvB.

concepts.intro: Coiling a current-carrying wire concentrates and shapes its magnetic field.
b: A solenoid produces a nearly uniform field inside, like a bar magnet's, and weak field outside.
Field strength grows with the current and with the number of turns per unit length.
Adding an iron core (an electromagnet) multiplies the field many times over.
Reversing the current reverses the north and south ends.
Electromagnets can be switched off, unlike permanent magnets — used in scrapyard cranes, relays, and maglev.

traps: Expecting the magnetic force to speed a charge up — it does zero work.
Forgetting the $\sinθ$ in $F = q v B \sinθ$ (no force when v is parallel to B).
Ignoring the minus sign in Lenz's law — the induced current always opposes the flux change.
Thinking a steady magnetic field through a stationary loop induces a current — it does not.
fms: Right-hand rule: fingers along velocity, curl to field, thumb is the force (flip for a negative charge).
Induction needs CHANGE — steady flux induces nothing.
Lenz = nature resists the change.
Step-up transformer trades current for voltage; power stays the same.

units.name: Simple Harmonic Motion

concepts.intro: SHM is back-and-forth motion driven by a restoring force proportional to displacement.
b: Condition: F = −k x (the restoring force points back toward equilibrium and grows with displacement).
Amplitude A is the maximum displacement; in ideal SHM it does not affect the period.
Period T is the time for one full cycle; frequency f = 1/T, in hertz.
Speed is maximum at equilibrium; acceleration is maximum at the turning points.
The motion repeats exactly in the absence of damping.

concepts.intro: A mass on an ideal spring is the archetypal harmonic oscillator.
b: $T = 2π \sqrt{m / k}$.
A stiffer spring (larger k) or a lighter mass gives a shorter period.
Quadrupling the mass doubles the period.
The equilibrium position is where the spring force balances gravity (for a vertical spring).
The period does not depend on the amplitude or on g.

concepts.intro: A small-angle pendulum is also SHM, with a strikingly simple period.
b: $T = 2π \sqrt{L / g}$ for small swings.
Depends only on length and g — not on mass or (for small angles) amplitude.
Quadrupling the length doubles the period.
A pendulum runs slow where g is smaller (e.g. on the Moon).
Large swing angles break the $T = 2π \sqrt{L/g}$ approximation.

concepts.intro: An oscillator continuously trades kinetic and potential energy while the total stays fixed.
b: Total mechanical energy = $0.5 k A^2$ for a mass–spring system.
All potential energy at the turning points; all kinetic energy at equilibrium.
Maximum speed $v_{max} = A \sqrt{k/m} = A ω$.
The energy is set by the amplitude and never exceeds its initial value.
At any point: $0.5 k x^2 + 0.5 m v^2 = 0.5 k A^2$.

concepts.intro: Real oscillators lose energy, and driving them at the right frequency builds large amplitudes.
b: Damping (friction, air resistance) gradually reduces the amplitude while barely changing the period.
Light damping decays slowly; heavy damping can stop oscillation altogether (overdamped).
Every system has natural frequencies at which it 'likes' to oscillate.
Resonance: driving a system at a natural frequency transfers energy efficiently and grows the amplitude.
Resonance explains shattered wine glasses, pushed swings, and some bridge failures.

traps: Thinking amplitude changes the period of ideal SHM — it does not.
Putting mass into the pendulum period — $T = 2π \sqrt{L/g}$ has no mass.
Saying acceleration is zero at the turning points — that is where it is largest.
Assuming damping quickly changes the period — it mainly shrinks the amplitude.
fms: Restoring force proportional to displacement → SHM; period is amplitude-independent.
Spring period grows with mass; pendulum period grows with length.
Fast at the middle, momentarily stopped at the ends.
Drive at a natural frequency → resonance → big amplitude.

units.name: Waves & Sound

concepts.intro: A wave transports energy through a medium without transporting the medium itself.
b: Transverse: particle motion is perpendicular to wave motion (string waves, light).
Longitudinal: particle motion is parallel to wave motion (sound).
Wave speed $v = f λ$.
Speed is set by the medium; changing frequency changes wavelength, not speed.
Amplitude relates to energy carried, not to speed.

concepts.intro: Waves reflect, refract, diffract, and interfere.
b: Reflection: a fixed end inverts a pulse; a free end does not.
Refraction: speed and wavelength change entering a new medium; frequency stays the same.
Diffraction: waves spread around edges and through gaps, most when the gap is near one wavelength.
Superposition: overlapping waves add displacement to displacement.
Constructive interference (in phase) builds amplitude; destructive (out of phase) cancels it.

concepts.intro: Confined waves form fixed node/antinode patterns at special frequencies.
b: A standing wave is two identical waves traveling in opposite directions.
Nodes stay still; antinodes oscillate with maximum amplitude.
String fixed at both ends: $L = n λ / 2$, with $f_n = n v / (2L)$.
Resonance: driving a system at a natural frequency gives a large-amplitude response.
Instruments select harmonics through their length and boundary conditions.

concepts.intro: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave that needs a medium.
b: Speed in air ≈ 343 m/s at 20°C; faster in liquids and solids; zero in vacuum.
Pitch corresponds to frequency; loudness corresponds to amplitude/intensity.
Human hearing runs roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Intensity falls off with an inverse-square law from a point source.
Beats: two close frequencies give $f_{beat} = |f_1 − f_2|$.

concepts.intro: Relative motion between a wave source and an observer shifts the observed frequency.
b: Source approaching → waves bunch up → higher observed frequency, shorter wavelength.
Source receding → waves stretch out → lower observed frequency.
Only motion along the line between source and observer matters.
Explains the pitch drop of a passing siren.
The same idea red-shifts light from receding galaxies.

traps: Saying a wave speeds up if you shake the source faster — frequency up means wavelength down, speed fixed by the medium.
Confusing nodes (no motion) with antinodes (maximum motion).
Thinking the Doppler effect changes the wave's actual speed.
Assuming sound can travel through a vacuum.
fms: $v = f λ$, and v belongs to the medium.
Fixed end flips the pulse; a both-ends-fixed string fits half-wavelengths.
Approaching source → higher pitch; receding → lower pitch.
Beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies.

units.name: Optics

concepts.intro: Light bouncing off surfaces obeys a simple angle rule and forms predictable images.
b: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal.
Plane mirror: image is virtual, upright, same size, as far behind as the object is in front.
Concave (converging) mirror: real, inverted image when the object is beyond the focal point.
Convex (diverging) mirror: always a virtual, upright, reduced image.
Mirror equation: $1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$; magnification $m = −d_i / d_o$.

concepts.intro: Light bends when it changes speed crossing between media.
b: Index of refraction $n = c / v_{medium}$; n ≥ 1, larger n means slower light.
Snell's law: $n_1 \sinθ_1 = n_2 \sinθ_2$.
Entering a denser (higher-n) medium bends light toward the normal.
Frequency and color do not change in refraction; speed and wavelength do.
A prism disperses white light because n varies slightly with wavelength.

concepts.intro: A lens forms images by refraction at its two curved surfaces.
b: Converging (convex) lens: real, inverted image for distant objects; magnifier for near objects.
Diverging (concave) lens: always virtual, upright, reduced.
Thin-lens equation matches the mirror equation: $1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$.
A positive image distance means a real image on the far side; negative means a virtual image.
The focal length depends on the lens shape and the index of refraction.

concepts.intro: Light going toward a less dense medium can be trapped entirely inside.
b: Occurs only going from higher n to lower n.
Happens when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle $θ_c$.
This is how optical fibers guide light over long distances.
Also produces mirages and the sparkle of cut diamonds.

concepts.l: Wave optics and the electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.intro: Interference and diffraction reveal light's wave nature; the spectrum orders it by wavelength.
b: A double slit produces bright/dark fringes from constructive/destructive interference.
A diffraction grating spreads light into sharp spectral orders.
Spectrum long to short wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
All electromagnetic waves travel at c ≈ $3.0 × 10^8 m/s$ in vacuum.
Higher frequency means shorter wavelength and more energy per photon.

traps: Measuring angles from the surface instead of from the normal.
Thinking a convex mirror or concave lens can make a real image — they cannot.
Saying refraction changes the light's frequency or color — only speed and wavelength change.
Expecting total internal reflection when going from low n to high n.
fms: Toward the normal when entering a slower (higher-n) medium.
Convex mirror and concave lens: always virtual, upright, smaller.
$1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$ for both mirrors and thin lenses.
TIR only high-n to low-n, past the critical angle.

units.name: Modern Physics

concepts.intro: Light also behaves as discrete packets of energy called photons.
b: Photon energy $E = h f = h c / λ$, with h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s.
The photoelectric effect ejects electrons only if the frequency exceeds a threshold, no matter the intensity.
This showed energy is delivered in quanta, which wave theory alone could not explain.
Above threshold, brighter light ejects more electrons; higher frequency gives each electron more kinetic energy.
$KE_{max} = h f − W$, where W is the metal's work function.

concepts.intro: Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels, and light carries the difference when they jump.
b: An electron absorbs a photon to jump up and emits a photon when it falls down.
The photon energy equals the difference between the two levels: $E_{photon} = E_{high} − E_{low}$.
Each element has a unique line spectrum — a fingerprint of its energy levels.
Emission spectra are bright lines; absorption spectra are dark lines at the same wavelengths.
Ground state is the lowest level; higher levels are excited states.

concepts.intro: Unstable nuclei decay by emitting particles or photons.
b: Alpha decay emits a helium-4 nucleus; mass number drops by 4, atomic number by 2.
Beta-minus decay emits an electron; a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic number rises by 1.
Gamma decay emits a high-energy photon; the nucleus loses energy but not particles.
Half-life is the time for half of a sample to decay; it is constant for a given isotope.
Mass number and charge are conserved when balancing a nuclear equation.

concepts.intro: Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing.
b: $E = m c^2$; because $c^2$ is enormous, a tiny mass change releases huge energy.
The mass of a nucleus is slightly less than its separate nucleons — the missing 'mass defect' is binding energy.
Nuclear reactions release far more energy per kilogram than chemical reactions.
Energy is still conserved overall; some rest mass simply converts to kinetic energy and radiation.
Units: 1 u of mass corresponds to about 931 MeV of energy.

concepts.intro: Both processes move nuclei toward the peak of the binding-energy curve, releasing energy.
b: Fission splits a heavy nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) into lighter fragments plus neutrons.
A chain reaction sustains fission when released neutrons trigger further splits.
Fusion joins light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier one; it powers the Sun.
Fusion releases more energy per nucleon but needs extreme temperature and pressure.
Iron-56 sits near the peak of binding energy per nucleon, so it releases energy in neither process.

traps: Thinking brighter light always ejects photoelectrons — the frequency must first exceed the threshold.
Saying an electron can occupy any energy in an atom — the levels are discrete.
Forgetting to conserve both mass number and atomic number in nuclear equations.
Confusing fission (splitting heavy nuclei) with fusion (joining light nuclei).
fms: Photon energy: E = h f — higher frequency, more energetic.
A spectral line is a jump between two fixed energy levels.
Alpha: −4 mass, −2 charge. Beta-minus: +1 charge, same mass number.
Mass defect = binding energy through $E = m c^2$.

flashcards.d: A base unit (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd) is defined on its own; a derived unit is a combination of base units, such as m/s for speed or N = kg·m/s².
The kilogram (kg), not the gram.
M × 10^n with 1 ≤ M < 10 and n an integer. Add/subtract with matching powers of 10; multiply → add exponents; divide → subtract exponents.
The power of 10 closest to a value: 1284 kg → 10^3 kg, but 8756 kg → 10^4 kg.
tera 10^12, giga 10^9, mega 10^6, kilo 10^3, centi 10^-2, milli 10^-3, micro 10^-6, nano 10^-9, pico 10^-12.
Precision is the smallest decimal place a measurement reports; accuracy is how close it is to the accepted value.
Systematic errors push all readings the same way (calibrate to fix); random errors scatter readings (average many trials).
|measured − accepted| / accepted × 100%.
A quantity with magnitude only: mass, distance, speed, time, energy, temperature.
A quantity with magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum.
The single vector equal to the sum of two or more vectors; found head-to-tail or by the parallelogram method.
For vectors A and B: |A − B| ≤ R ≤ A + B; the maximum is at 0° between them and the minimum at 180°.
R = √(A² + B²), direction from tanθ = B/A.
A_x = A cosθ and A_y = A sinθ, with θ measured from the horizontal.
The vector with the same magnitude as the resultant but the opposite direction; it makes the net vector zero.
Distance is total path length (scalar); displacement is the straight-line change in position with direction (vector).
Speed = total distance / total time (scalar); velocity = displacement / time (vector).
Speed and direction at a single instant, like a speedometer reading plus a compass heading.
Motion at constant velocity: the same speed in the same direction. Horizontal line on a v–t graph; straight sloped line on a d–t graph.
The velocity. Its size is the speed; a positive slope means motion in the positive direction, a negative slope the negative direction.
The distance traveled. Split it into rectangles and triangles to compute it.
The rate of change of velocity, a = Δv/Δt, in m/s². A vector: it can come from a change in speed, direction, or both.
Acceleration opposite to the velocity, so the object slows down. Not the same as 'negative acceleration', which only describes direction.

flashcards.d: Instantaneous: slope of the tangent at one point. Average: slope of the straight line joining the start and end points.
30-story building ≈ 10² m; football field ≈ 100 m; little finger ≈ 0.01 m wide; pencil ≈ 5 × 10⁻³ kg; adult ≈ 70 kg.
A fixed ratio between arrow length and magnitude, e.g. 1 mm = 2 m/s. If 15 mm = 30 m/s, then 20 m/s = 10 mm.
Velocities add as vectors: 4.0 m/s forward on a 2.0 m/s bus is 6.0 m/s relative to the street; toward the back, 2.0 m/s the other way.
For vectors A and B: |A − B| ≤ R ≤ A + B. Largest at 0°, smallest at 180°.

flashcards.t: Average speed of a round trip
flashcards.d: Total distance ÷ total time, not the average of the two speeds (150 km at 60 km/h and back at 75 km/h ≈ 67 km/h).
sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
V = πr²h, using the radius (half the diameter); 1 cm³ = 1 mL.
Vector change in position, Δx = xf − xi. Can be zero even after a long trip if you return to start.
Scalar total path length traveled; always ≥ magnitude of displacement.
The slope of the tangent line to a position-time graph at one instant.
Vector rate of change of velocity, a = Δv/Δt. Occurs whenever speed OR direction changes.
9.8 m/s² downward near Earth's surface, same for all masses (ignoring air resistance).
vf = vi + at
Δx = vi·t + ½at²
vf² = vi² + 2aΔx
Horizontal velocity stays constant; vertical velocity changes due to gravity — the two directions are independent.
An object at rest or in constant-velocity motion stays that way unless acted on by a net external force (inertia).
Fnet = ma — acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.
For every action force, there's an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a DIFFERENT object.
Contact force perpendicular to a surface, preventing objects from passing through each other.
Friction that resists the START of sliding; maximum value fs,max = μs·FN.
Friction that resists sliding once motion has begun: fk = μk·FN.
A diagram isolating one object, showing every external force acting on it as an arrow.
The gravitational force on an object, Fg = mg — not the same as mass.
p = mv, a vector describing an object's quantity of motion.
J = FΔt = Δp — the change in momentum caused by a force acting over time.
In an isolated system, total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after.
Momentum AND kinetic energy are both conserved; objects bounce apart without permanent deformation.
Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not — some converts to heat/sound/deformation.
W = Fd cosθ — energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement.
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: Wnet = ΔKE.
KE = ½mv² — energy of motion, always non-negative.
KEi + PEi = KEf + PEf when only conservative forces (gravity, springs) act on the system.
ac = v²/r, always directed toward the center of a circular path.
Fc = mv²/r — the net inward force needed for circular motion, supplied by tension, gravity, friction, or normal force.
Fg = Gm1m2/r² — attractive force between any two masses, inverse-square with distance.
T² ∝ r³ — orbital period squared is proportional to orbital radius cubed.
v = √(Gm1/r) — depends on the central mass and orbital radius, not the satellite's own mass.
Distance between two successive identical points on a wave (e.g., crest to crest).
Number of complete wave cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
v = fλ — determined by the medium, not by frequency or amplitude alone.
Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of energy travel (e.g., light, waves on a string).
Particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy travel, with compressions and rarefactions (e.g., sound).
In-phase waves add together, producing a larger amplitude.
Apparent shift in observed frequency due to relative motion between a wave source and observer.
Fe = kq1q2/r² — the electric force between two point charges, inverse-square with distance.
E = F/q — force per unit positive test charge; points away from + charges, toward − charges.
V = IR — relates voltage, current, and resistance.
Same current everywhere; total resistance = sum of individual resistances.
Same voltage across every branch; total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistor.
P = IV = I²R = V²/R — rate of electrical energy transfer.

flashcards.t: Magnetic force on a moving charge
flashcards.d: F = qvB sinθ — zero if velocity is parallel to the field, maximum if perpendicular.
Used to find the direction of a magnetic field around a current, or the force on a moving charge in a field.
A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an EMF (voltage) in that loop.
Induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in flux that created it.
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
n = c/v — ratio of light's speed in a vacuum to its speed in a medium; always ≥ 1.
n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2 — relates the bending of light at a boundary between two media.
Occurs when light travels from a denser to less dense medium beyond the critical angle — all light reflects, none refracts out.
Thicker in the middle; focuses parallel rays to a real focal point.
1/f = 1/do + 1/di — relates focal length, object distance, and image distance.
Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons from a metal; explained by treating light as photons, E = hf.
W0 — the minimum energy needed to eject an electron from a metal's surface.
λ = h/p — matter waves; all moving matter has an associated wavelength.
The time for half of a radioactive sample to decay; decay is exponential, not linear.
Nucleus emits a helium nucleus (2p+2n); mass number −4, atomic number −2; stopped by paper.
Nucleus emits high-energy EM radiation; no change in mass or atomic number; needs lead/concrete to stop.
A neutron converts to a proton (emitting an electron); mass number unchanged, atomic number ±1; stopped by aluminum.
Combining light nuclei into a heavier one, releasing large amounts of energy — powers the Sun.
v = 2πr/T — speed of an object moving in a circle of radius r with period T.
Planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.
A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times — planets move faster near the Sun.
6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² — the proportionality constant in Newton's law of universal gravitation.
Charge is quantized: q = ne, where e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C is the elementary charge.
Total charge in an isolated system is constant — charge is transferred, never created or destroyed.
A material property in R = ρL/A; resistance increases with length, decreases with cross-sectional area.
F = BIL sinθ — the magnetic force on a wire of length L carrying current I in field B.
Converts electrical energy to mechanical energy using the force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.
Converts mechanical energy to electrical energy by rotating a coil within a magnetic field, inducing an EMF.
Horizontal velocity is constant (a_x = 0); vertical motion is free fall (a_y = -g). The two axes share only the time t.
R = v0^2 sin(2*theta) / g. Maximum at theta = 45 degrees; complementary angles give equal range.
t = 2 v0 sin(theta) / g, which is twice the time to reach maximum height.
Motion with gravity as the only force. All objects fall with the same acceleration, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward (Galileo, not Aristotle).

flashcards.t: Reaction time from a dropped ruler
flashcards.d: t = √(2d/g), where d is how far the ruler fell before you caught it.
N = mg cos(theta); the gravity component along the incline is mg sin(theta).
N = m(g + a) accelerating up, N = m(g - a) accelerating down; N = 0 in free fall.
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = 0.5 m v_f^2 - 0.5 m v_i^2.
Impulse J = F_avg * delta t = change in momentum delta p. Units: N*s = kg*m/s.
Objects stick together: m1 v1 + m2 v2 = (m1 + m2) v_f. Momentum conserved, kinetic energy is not.
P = W/t = energy/time (watts). Also P = F v for a force moving an object at speed v.
v = sqrt(G M / r). Larger orbital radius means slower orbital speed and a longer period.
The spacecraft and astronaut are in free fall together, so there is no normal force between them; gravity is still present.
v = f * lambda. Speed is fixed by the medium; changing frequency changes wavelength, not speed.
Source approaching -> higher observed frequency (shorter wavelength); source receding -> lower observed frequency.

flashcards.t: Standing wave on a string (both ends fixed)
flashcards.d: L = n * lambda / 2; harmonic frequencies f_n = n * v / (2L), n = 1, 2, 3, ...
Series: R_total = R1 + R2 + ... (increases). Parallel: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... (decreases, less than the smallest).
P = I V = I^2 R = V^2 / R, measured in watts.
F = q v B sin(theta), perpendicular to both v and B. Zero when v is parallel to B; maximum when perpendicular.
Induced EMF = - N * (change in magnetic flux) / (change in time). A changing flux is required.
The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produced it (energy conservation).
V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p. Ideal power is conserved, so V_p I_p = V_s I_s.
n = c / v_medium (>= 1). Larger n means slower light and more bending toward the normal on entry.
n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2). Frequency is unchanged in refraction; speed and wavelength change.
Occurs going from higher n to lower n at angles beyond the critical angle: sin(theta_c) = n2 / n1.
E = h f = h c / lambda, with h = 6.63e-34 J*s. Higher frequency means more energy per photon.
Electrons are ejected only if the light frequency exceeds a threshold. KE_max = h f - W (work function).
tau = r F sin(theta) = (perpendicular lever arm) x force, in N*m. A force through the axis gives zero torque.
Net torque = I * alpha, where I is the moment of inertia and alpha is the angular acceleration.
Rotational 'mass'; depends on mass and its distance from the axis (proportional to r^2). Hoop MR^2, disk 0.5 MR^2, solid sphere 0.4 MR^2.
L = I omega. Conserved when no external torque acts: I1 omega1 = I2 omega2 (skater pulling in arms spins faster).
Same equations as linear motion with x -> theta, v -> omega, a -> alpha. Also s = r theta, v = r omega, a_t = r alpha.
Sum of torques = 0 and sum of forces = 0. Torques may be taken about any convenient point.
A rolling object has KE = 0.5 m v^2 + 0.5 I omega^2, so it accelerates down a ramp slower than a sliding one.
A restoring force proportional to displacement: F = -k x. The period is independent of amplitude.
T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k). Stiffer spring or lighter mass gives a shorter period; independent of g and amplitude.
T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) for small angles. Depends only on length and g, not on mass or amplitude.
Total energy = 0.5 k A^2. All potential energy at the turning points, all kinetic energy at equilibrium.
v_max = A sqrt(k/m) = A omega, occurring as the oscillator passes through equilibrium.

flashcards.t: Where acceleration is largest in SHM
flashcards.d: At the turning points (maximum displacement), because acceleration is proportional to -x. It is zero at equilibrium.
Energy loss (friction, air resistance) that gradually reduces amplitude while barely changing the period.
Driving a system at one of its natural frequencies transfers energy efficiently and builds a large amplitude.

quiz.q: The SI unit of mass is the:
quiz.e: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass; the gram is a smaller metric unit.

quiz.q: Which of these is a derived unit rather than a base unit?
quiz.e: The newton is defined as kg·m/s², a combination of base units.

quiz.q: Which of these is an SI base unit?
quiz.e: The ampere (electric current) is one of the seven base units; the others listed are derived.

quiz.q: A student solves F = ma with m = 5 kg and a = 10 m/s² and writes only "F = 50". Why does the answer lose credit?
quiz.e: 5 × 10 = 50 is correct, but a physics answer needs its unit: 50 N.

quiz.q: Which prefix stands for 10^12?
quiz.e: tera = 10^12; pico is 10^-12.

quiz.q: Which prefix stands for 10^3?
quiz.e: kilo means one thousand, 10^3.

quiz.q: A megawatt is:
quiz.e: mega = 10^6.

quiz.q: 5.0 ms (milliseconds) expressed in seconds is:
quiz.e: milli = 10^-3.

quiz.q: 3.5 km expressed in meters is:
250 nm expressed in meters is:
The average distance from the Sun to Mars is 227 800 000 000 m. In scientific notation this is:
quiz.e: Move the decimal 11 places left: 2.278 × 10^11 m.

quiz.q: 0.000 000 103 m written in scientific notation is:
quiz.e: Move the decimal 7 places right: 1.03 × 10^-7 m.

quiz.q: 2 003 000 000 m written in scientific notation is:
quiz.e: Nine places to the left gives 2.003 × 10^9 m; keep the zeros between digits.

quiz.q: What is the order of magnitude of 72 meters per second?
quiz.e: 72 = 7.2 × 10^1, and 7.2 is closer to 10 than to 1, so the order of magnitude is 10^2.

quiz.q: What is the order of magnitude of 8756 kg?
quiz.e: 8756 = 8.756 × 10^3, and 8.756 is closer to 10 than to 1, so it is on the order of 10^4 kg.

quiz.q: What is the order of magnitude of 8.2 × 10^-9 m?
quiz.e: 8.2 is closer to 10 than 1, so round up to 10 × 10^-9 = 10^-8 m.
Same power of 10, so add the M values and keep the exponent.

3.14 + 9.36 = 12.50 × 10^-5, which in proper scientific notation is 1.250 × 10^-4.
8 / 2 = 4 and 6 − (−3) = 9; the units m³/m² leave m.
6.5 / 3.4 = 1.9 and 5 − 3 = 2; this is a density.

quiz.q: Which is the most likely mass of a high school student?
quiz.e: A typical teenager has a mass around 60 kg.

quiz.q: The height of an average adult is approximately:
quiz.e: Adults are a little under 2 m tall.

quiz.q: The length of a high school physics classroom is closest to:
quiz.e: A classroom is on the order of 10 m long.

quiz.q: Which measurement of an average classroom door is closest to 1 meter?
quiz.e: A door is roughly 0.9 m wide; its height is about 2 m and its thickness a few cm.

quiz.q: The weight of an apple is closest to:
quiz.e: An apple has a mass of about 0.1 kg, so its weight is about 1 N.

quiz.q: The measurement 24.962 s is precise to the nearest:
quiz.e: The last digit sits in the thousandths place.

quiz.q: How many significant figures are in 0.00420 kg?
quiz.e: Leading zeros do not count; 4, 2, and the trailing 0 after the decimal do.

quiz.q: How many significant figures are in 3000 K (no decimal point)?
quiz.e: Trailing zeros with no decimal point are not significant.

quiz.q: The average of several measurements of a mass is 48.60 g and the accepted value is 48.75 g. The percent error is about:
A thermometer reads 5°C in an ice-and-water mixture that is really at 0°C. This is what kind of error?
quiz.e: Every reading is off the same way, which is systematic error; calibrating the thermometer fixes it.

quiz.q: Random errors in a measurement are best reduced by:
quiz.e: Random fluctuations tend to cancel in an average of many trials.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a scalar?
quiz.e: Temperature has magnitude only; the others include a direction.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a vector?
quiz.e: Momentum has both magnitude and direction.

quiz.q: In a vector diagram, the length of the arrow represents the vector's:
quiz.e: Arrow length is proportional to magnitude; the arrowhead shows direction.

quiz.q: Two forces are called concurrent when they:
o: act on the same point at the same time
quiz.e: Concurrent means acting together on one point.

quiz.q: Two concurrent forces of 3 N and 4 N act at 90° to each other. The magnitude of the resultant is:
An object is displaced 12 meters to the right and then 16 meters upward. The magnitude of its total displacement is:
An object is displaced 3 meters west and then 4 meters south. The magnitude of its displacement is:
A girl swims directly across a 15 m wide stream and ends up 15 m downstream. The magnitude of her displacement is closest to:
A boat heads directly east across a river at 12 m/s while the current flows due south at 5.0 m/s. The magnitude of the boat's resultant velocity is:
Two forces of 100 N and 25 N act concurrently on an object. Their resultant could be:
quiz.e: The resultant must lie between 100 − 25 = 75 N and 100 + 25 = 125 N; only 100 N fits.

quiz.q: The resultant of two concurrent forces is a minimum when the angle between them is:
quiz.e: Opposite forces cancel as much as possible.

quiz.q: As the angle between two concurrent forces of 5.0 N and 7.0 N increases from 0° to 180°, the magnitude of their resultant changes from:
quiz.e: At 0° the forces add (12 N); at 180° they subtract (2.0 N).

quiz.q: Two 10-N concurrent forces have a resultant of zero. The angle between them must be:
quiz.e: Only equal and opposite forces sum to zero.

quiz.q: A force of 3 N and a force of 5 N act concurrently to produce a resultant of 8 N. The angle between them must be:
quiz.e: 8 = 3 + 5 only when the forces point the same way.

quiz.q: Two concurrent forces have a maximum resultant of 45 N and a minimum resultant of 5 N. What are their magnitudes?
quiz.e: A + B = 45 and A − B = 5, so A = 25 N and B = 20 N.

quiz.q: A 6.0 N force and an 8.0 N force act concurrently at 90° to each other. The magnitude of the resultant is:
Which set of three concurrent forces could NOT produce equilibrium?
quiz.e: For equilibrium the largest force must not exceed the sum of the other two; 1 + 3 < 5.

quiz.q: A 60. N force acts 30° above the horizontal. Its horizontal component is closest to:
A 100 N force acts 30° above the horizontal. Its vertical component is:
A force of 28.0 N is applied to a lawn-roller handle held 45° above the horizontal. The force moving the roller forward is:
A resultant force of 10. N is made of two perpendicular components. If one component is 6.0 N, the other is:
A block of weight F_g rests on a 30° incline. The component of its weight parallel to the incline is:
A lawn mower is pushed with a constant force along its handle. As the angle between the handle and the horizontal increases, the horizontal component of the force:
quiz.e: Horizontal component = F cosθ, and cosθ decreases as θ increases.

quiz.q: A 300. N force acts on a shovel handle at 60° above the ground. Its vertical component is closest to:
A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m track. Her distance and displacement are:
quiz.e: She travels 400 m along the path but ends where she started.

quiz.q: A car drives 30 km east and then 40 km north. Its displacement has a magnitude of:
quiz.e: √(30² + 40²) = 50 km, while the distance is 70 km.

quiz.q: A car travels 120 m in 8.0 s. Its average speed is:
A motorist drives 60 km in the first hour and 40 km in the second hour. Her average speed is:
quiz.e: Total distance 100 km divided by total time 2 h.

quiz.q: A student walks 40 m east in 20 s and then 40 m west in 20 s. Her average velocity for the whole trip is:
quiz.e: The net displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero.

quiz.q: For the same trip (40 m east then 40 m west in 40 s total), her average speed is:
quiz.e: Average speed = total distance / total time = 80 m / 40 s.

quiz.q: A hiker's displacement is 150 m north in 30 s. His average velocity is:
quiz.e: A velocity needs a direction: 150 / 30 = 5.0 m/s north.

quiz.q: Which quantity includes a direction?
quiz.e: Velocity is a vector; speed, distance, and time are scalars.

quiz.q: The reading on a car's speedometer at one moment is the car's:
quiz.e: The speedometer gives speed at that instant, with no direction.

quiz.q: An object's velocity is −4 m/s. This means it is:
o: moving in the negative direction at 4 m/s
quiz.e: The sign gives direction; the speed is 4 m/s.

quiz.q: A cyclist rides at a steady 8.0 m/s for 15 s. The distance covered is:
How long does it take to travel 300 km at a constant 60 km/h?
Which statement about distance and displacement is always true?
o: Displacement is always greater than distance
The magnitude of the displacement is never greater than the distance
quiz.e: The straight line from start to finish is the shortest path.

quiz.q: The dot product of two vectors is:
quiz.e: A·B = AB cosθ is a single number; the cross product is the vector one.

quiz.q: The cross product of two parallel vectors is:
quiz.e: |A×B| = AB sinθ, and sin 0° = 0.

quiz.q: To subtract vector B from vector A, you can:
o: add a vector with B's length pointing the opposite way

quiz.q: A girl walks 10. meters north to a drinking fountain and then 30. meters south to an art classroom. Her total displacement from the start is:
quiz.e: Taking north as positive: +10 − 30 = −20, so the displacement is 20. m south (the distance walked is 40. m).

quiz.q: A projectile is fired at 120. m/s at an angle θ above the horizontal. If its initial horizontal speed is 55 m/s, the angle θ is approximately:
quiz.e: v_x = v cosθ, so cosθ = 55/120 = 0.458 and θ ≈ 63°.

quiz.q: A student walks four blocks south, five blocks west, and four more blocks south. Compared with the distance she walks, the magnitude of her displacement from home to school is:
quiz.e: She walks 13 blocks, but her displacement is √(8² + 5²) ≈ 9.4 blocks; the straight line is always the shortest path.

quiz.q: A vector makes an angle θ with the horizontal. Its horizontal and vertical components have equal magnitudes when θ is:
quiz.e: A cosθ = A sinθ only when tanθ = 1, which is at 45°.

quiz.q: A car travels 90. m due north in 15 s, then turns around and travels 40. m due south in 5.0 s. The magnitude of its average velocity for the 20-s interval is:
quiz.e: Displacement = 90. − 40. = 50. m over 20 s = 2.5 m/s. (6.5 m/s would be the average speed, 130 m / 20 s.)

quiz.q: In a 4.0-km race, a runner covers the four 1.0-km sections in 5.9, 6.2, 6.3, and 6.0 minutes. Her average speed for the race is about:
quiz.e: Total time = 24.4 min, so 4.0 km / 24.4 min ≈ 0.16 km/min.

quiz.q: A golf ball is hit at 15 m/s at 35° above the horizontal. The vertical component of its initial velocity is:
quiz.e: 15 sin 35° ≈ 8.6 m/s (the horizontal component is 15 cos 35° ≈ 12 m/s).

quiz.q: The average speed of a runner in a 400.-m race is 8.0 m/s. How long did the race take?
An object travels for 8.00 s at an average speed of 160. m/s. The distance traveled is:
An object moves a distance of 10 m in 5 s. Its average speed is:
A moving body must undergo a change of:
quiz.e: Motion means position changes with time; a body moving at constant velocity has no change in velocity or acceleration, and a straight-line mover has no change in direction.

quiz.q: What is the largest number of components a single force can be resolved into?
quiz.e: A vector can be replaced by any number of vectors that add up to it; two perpendicular components are just the most useful choice.

quiz.q: A man walks 17 m east and then 17 m south. The magnitude of his displacement is:
A worker pulls a cart with a rope. The worker's pull can best be described as a force having:
quiz.e: Force is a vector, so a complete description needs a size and a direction.

quiz.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
quiz.e: Force has direction; mass, time, and distance are scalars.

quiz.q: A 5.0 N force could have perpendicular components of:
quiz.e: The components must satisfy √(A² + B²) = 5.0, and 3.0² + 4.0² = 5.0².

quiz.q: Two 10.0 N forces act concurrently on a point at an angle of 180° to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is:
quiz.e: Equal forces pointing in opposite directions cancel.

quiz.q: As the angle between two concurrent forces of 10 N and 12 N changes from 180° to 0°, the magnitude of their resultant changes from:
quiz.e: At 180° the forces subtract (12 − 10 = 2.0 N); at 0° they add (22 N).

quiz.q: Two concurrent forces act at right angles. If one force is 40 N and their resultant is 50 N, the other force is:
A 5.0 N force and a 12 N force act at right angles on point P. The magnitude of their resultant is:
Two 30.-N forces act concurrently on an object. The resultant is also 30. N when the angle between the forces is:
