quiz.e: With equal forces, R = 2F cos(θ/2); R = F requires cos(θ/2) = 0.5, so θ = 120°.

quiz.q: A constant force F is applied to a mass on a frictionless horizontal surface at an angle θ above the horizontal. As θ increases, the mass's horizontal acceleration:
quiz.e: The horizontal component F cosθ shrinks as θ grows, so a = F cosθ / m decreases.

quiz.q: A skater speeds up uniformly from 2.0 m/s to 7.0 m/s over a distance of 12 m. What is the magnitude of her acceleration?
quiz.e: No time is given, so use v² = v₀² + 2ad: 7.0² = 2.0² + 2a(12), so 49 = 4 + 24a and a = 45 ÷ 24 ≈ 1.9 m/s².

quiz.q: A wagon's speed increases uniformly from 2.5 m/s to 9.0 m/s in 3.0 s as it rolls down a hill. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
quiz.e: a = Δv ÷ t = (9.0 − 2.5) m/s ÷ 3.0 s = 6.5 ÷ 3.0 ≈ 2.2 m/s². 6.5 m/s² forgets to divide by the time.

quiz.q: An object moving at 4.0 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2.0 m/s² in its direction of motion for 5.0 m. What is its final speed?
quiz.e: v² = v₀² + 2ad = 4.0² + 2(2.0)(5.0) = 16 + 20 = 36, so v = √36 = 6.0 m/s. 36 m/s forgets the square root.

quiz.q: Which statement about an object with zero acceleration is true?
o: The object may be in motion.
The object must be at rest.
The object must be slowing down.
The object's velocity must be changing.
quiz.e: Zero acceleration means the velocity isn't changing, not that it is zero. The object can be at rest or moving at a constant velocity.

quiz.q: Acceleration is a vector quantity that represents the time-rate of change in:
quiz.e: Acceleration = Δv ÷ Δt. The rate of change of position is velocity, not acceleration.

quiz.q: On a velocity–time graph, an object moving with constant velocity appears as:
quiz.e: Constant velocity means v doesn't change as time passes, so every point sits at the same height: a horizontal line.

quiz.q: On a distance–time graph, an object in uniform motion appears as:
o: a straight line with constant slope
quiz.e: Equal distances are covered in equal times, so distance grows linearly with time. A horizontal d–t line would mean the object isn't moving.

quiz.q: The slope of a distance–time graph represents the object's:
quiz.e: Slope = rise/run = Δd/Δt, which is velocity. The slope of a v–t graph is acceleration.

quiz.q: A position–time graph is a straight line with a negative slope. The object is:
o: moving at constant speed in the negative direction
speeding up in the positive direction
quiz.e: A straight line means constant velocity; the negative slope means that velocity points in the negative direction.

quiz.q: An object moves at a constant 6.0 m/s for 5.0 s. On its v–t graph, the area under the line equals:
o: 0 m, because the velocity is constant
quiz.e: The area under a v–t graph is distance: a rectangle 6.0 m/s tall and 5.0 s wide has area 30 m.

quiz.q: A distance–time graph is a straight line from 0 m at t = 0 to 40. m at t = 8.0 s. The object's speed is:
quiz.e: Speed = slope = 40. m ÷ 8.0 s = 5.0 m/s. 0.20 m/s divides the wrong way.

quiz.q: A car slows uniformly from 20. m/s to 5.0 m/s in 3.0 s. Its acceleration is:
quiz.e: a = (v_f − v_i)/t = (5.0 − 20.)/3.0 = −5.0 m/s². The minus sign shows the acceleration opposes the motion. −15 forgets to divide by time.

quiz.q: Deceleration means that an object's acceleration:
o: points the same way as its velocity
quiz.e: Deceleration is slowing down, which happens whenever a and v point in opposite directions. A negative acceleration only slows the object if the velocity is positive.

quiz.q: An object has a negative velocity and a negative acceleration. It is:
o: speeding up in the negative direction
quiz.e: Velocity and acceleration point the same way (both negative), so the speed increases, in the negative direction.

quiz.q: A car rounds a curve at a constant 15 m/s. Is it accelerating?
o: Yes, because the direction of its velocity is changing
No, because its speed is constant
No, because acceleration needs a change in speed
quiz.e: Velocity is a vector. Changing its direction changes the velocity, and any change in velocity is acceleration.

quiz.q: A cart starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3.0 m/s² for 6.0 s. Its final speed is:
A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.0 m/s² for 5.0 s. How far does it travel?
quiz.e: From rest, d = ½at² = ½(2.0)(5.0)² = 25 m. 50 m forgets the ½; 10 m is the final speed's number.

quiz.q: Which constant-acceleration equation should you use when the time is not given?
quiz.e: v_f² = v_0² + 2ad is the only one of these with no t in it.

quiz.q: The SI unit of acceleration is:
quiz.e: Acceleration is change in velocity (m/s) per second, so its unit is (m/s)/s = m/s².

quiz.q: A position–time graph that curves (is not a straight line) shows that the object's:
quiz.e: A curve means the slope, which is the velocity, changes from point to point: nonuniform motion.

quiz.q: On a curved position–time graph, the instantaneous velocity at a point is:
o: the slope of the tangent line at that point
the slope of the line from the start to that point
the area under the curve up to that point
the height of the curve at that point
quiz.e: The tangent slope gives the velocity at that instant; the slope of a line joining two points gives the average velocity between them.

quiz.q: On a position–time graph, the average velocity for a whole trip is the slope of:
o: the straight line joining the starting and ending points
the tangent at the starting point
the steepest part of the curve
the tangent at the ending point
quiz.e: Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time, which is the slope of the straight line (secant) between the endpoints.

quiz.q: At one point on a position–time curve the tangent line is horizontal. At that instant the object is:
quiz.e: A horizontal tangent has zero slope, so the instantaneous velocity is zero: the object has stopped, often just as it turns around.

quiz.q: The slope of a velocity–time graph represents:
quiz.e: Slope = Δv/Δt, which is acceleration. The area under a v–t graph is distance.

quiz.q: A v–t graph is a straight line from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 12 m/s at t = 4.0 s. The object's acceleration and distance traveled are:
quiz.e: Acceleration = slope = 12 ÷ 4.0 = 3.0 m/s². Distance = area of the triangle = ½ × 4.0 s × 12 m/s = 24 m (48 m forgets the ½).

quiz.q: Compared with y = mx + b, the equation v = v_0 + at shows that on a v–t graph:
o: the slope is a and the vertical intercept is v_0
the slope is v_0 and the intercept is a
the slope is t and the intercept is v
the slope is v and the intercept is t
quiz.e: Write it as v = (a)t + v_0: v plays y, t plays x, a is the slope m, and v_0 is the intercept b.

quiz.q: The height of a 30-story building is approximately:
quiz.e: Each story is about 3 m, so 30 × 3 m ≈ 90 m, which is closest to 10² m.

quiz.q: The length of a football field is closest to:
quiz.e: A football field is about 100 m. 1000 dm = 100 m; 1000 cm is only 10 m and 1000 mm is 1 m.

quiz.q: What is the approximate width of a person's little finger?
quiz.e: A little finger is about 1 cm wide, and 1 cm = 0.01 m.

quiz.q: What is the approximate mass of a pencil?
quiz.e: A pencil is about 5 g. Since 1000 g = 1 kg, 5 g = 0.005 kg = 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg.

quiz.q: Two displacements of 3 m and 4 m are added. What are the largest and smallest possible resultants?
quiz.e: Largest when they point the same way (3 + 4 = 7 m); smallest when they point opposite ways (4 − 3 = 1 m). 5 m is the resultant at 90°.

quiz.q: As the angle between two displacement vectors increases from 0° to 180°, their resultant:
o: decreases from A + B to |A − B|
increases from |A − B| to A + B
quiz.e: At 0° the vectors add fully; as they turn apart they cancel more and more, until at 180° only the difference is left.

quiz.q: A vector drawn 15 mm long represents a velocity of 30 m/s. How long should a vector representing 20 m/s be?
quiz.e: The scale is 15 mm ÷ 30 m/s = 0.5 mm per m/s, so 20 m/s × 0.5 mm = 10 mm.

quiz.q: You ride a bus moving at 2.0 m/s and walk toward the front at 4.0 m/s relative to the bus. Your speed relative to the street is:
quiz.e: Both velocities point the same way, so they add: 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0 m/s relative to the street.

quiz.q: On the same bus (2.0 m/s), you walk toward the back at 4.0 m/s relative to the bus. Your velocity relative to the street is:
quiz.e: Now the velocities point opposite ways: 4.0 − 2.0 = 2.0 m/s in your walking direction, toward the back.

quiz.q: In 1999 Hicham El Guerrouj ran a mile (1609 m) in 3 min 43.13 s. His average speed was about:
quiz.e: Convert the time to seconds: 3 × 60 + 43.13 = 223.13 s. Then 1609 m ÷ 223.13 s ≈ 7.21 m/s.

quiz.q: A motorist drives 150 km in 2.5 h and makes the return trip in 2.0 h. Her average speeds going and returning were:
quiz.e: Going: 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Returning: 150 ÷ 2.0 = 75 km/h.

quiz.q: For that whole round trip (150 km each way, 2.5 h and 2.0 h), the average speed is closest to:
quiz.e: Total distance ÷ total time = 300 km ÷ 4.5 h ≈ 66.7 km/h. Averaging 60 and 75 (67.5) is wrong because she spent longer at the slower speed.

quiz.q: A hiker walks 5.0 km in the first hour and 4.4 km in the second hour. Her average speed for the first two hours is:
The same hiker (5.0 km, then 4.4 km) rests during the third hour. Her average speed for the first three hours is:
quiz.e: Resting still counts as time: 9.4 km ÷ 3 h ≈ 3.1 km/h.

quiz.q: She then walks 4.6 km in the fourth hour. Her average speed for the whole 4-hour period is:
quiz.e: Total distance = 5.0 + 4.4 + 4.6 = 14.0 km over 4 h = 3.5 km/h. 4.67 km/h leaves out the hour of rest.

quiz.q: The resultant of two forces acting on the same point at the same time is greatest when the angle between them is:
quiz.e: At 0° the forces point the same way and add fully (A + B).

quiz.q: Two concurrent forces of 2.0 N and 1.5 N act at right angles. The magnitude of their resultant is:
Find the components of a helicopter's velocity of 95 km/h at 35° above the ground.
An aircraft climbs at a steady 200. m/s at 20° above the horizontal. The horizontal and vertical components of its velocity are:
A bus travels 23.0 km on a straight road 30° north of east. The east and north components of its displacement are:
quiz.e: East = 23.0 cos 30° ≈ 19.9 km; north = 23.0 sin 30° = 11.5 km.

quiz.q: What are the components of a vector of magnitude 1.5 m at 35° from the positive x-axis?
A car moves at 50 km/h in a direction 60° north of east (x = east, y = north). Which component of its velocity is larger?
o: y (north): about 43 km/h vs. 25 km/h east
x (east): about 43 km/h vs. 25 km/h north
quiz.e: vx = 50 cos 60° = 25 km/h; vy = 50 sin 60° ≈ 43 km/h. More than 45° from the x-axis means the y-component wins.

quiz.q: A 4 N force points east and a 3 N force points north. Their resultant is:
o: 5 N at about 37° north of east
5 N at about 53° north of east
quiz.e: R = √(4² + 3²) = 5 N; θ = tan⁻¹(3/4) ≈ 37° north of east. 53° measures from north instead.

quiz.q: A velocity of 80. m/s is directed 30° above the horizontal. The magnitude of its vertical component is:
quiz.e: vy = 80. sin 30° = 80.(0.50) = 40. m/s. 69 m/s is the horizontal component.

quiz.q: In Lab 1.1, a can measures 6.6 cm across and 12.2 cm tall. Its capacity is about:
quiz.e: V = πr²h with r = 3.3 cm: π(3.3)²(12.2) ≈ 417 cm³ = 417 mL. Using the 6.6 cm diameter as r gives about 1670 mL.

quiz.q: A student walks halfway around a 30 m × 40 m rectangular field, from one corner to the opposite corner. Her distance and displacement are:
quiz.e: Distance = 30 + 40 = 70 m along the path; displacement = √(30² + 40²) = 50 m, straight across.

quiz.q: Solving d = ½at² for t gives:
quiz.e: Multiply both sides by 2 and divide by a to get t² = 2d/a, then take the square root.

quiz.q: In a right triangle, sin θ equals:
quiz.e: SOH: sine = opposite over hypotenuse. CAH gives cosine and TOA gives tangent.

quiz.q: A speed of 72 km/h equals:
quiz.e: 72 km/h × 1000 m/km ÷ 3600 s/h = 20 m/s (dividing by 3.6). 259 multiplies by 3.6 instead.

quiz.q: A runner moves 50 m east then 20 m west. What is the runner's displacement?
quiz.e: Displacement = 50 east − 20 east(since west is −) = 50 − 20 = 30 m east. Distance would be 70 m, but displacement is 30 m east.

quiz.q: What is the total distance traveled by the runner in the previous scenario?
quiz.e: Distance is the total path length: 50 m + 20 m = 70 m, regardless of direction.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a vector?
quiz.e: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector. Distance, speed, and time are scalars.

quiz.q: On a position-time graph, the slope represents:
quiz.e: Slope of an x-t graph = $Δx/Δt =$ velocity.

quiz.q: On a velocity-time graph, the area under the curve represents:
quiz.e: Area under a v-t graph = displacement (since $Δx = v·t$ for each small interval).

quiz.q: An object has a positive velocity and a negative acceleration. The object is:
quiz.e: When velocity and acceleration have opposite signs, the object is slowing down (decelerating).

quiz.q: A car accelerates from rest at 4 m/s² for 5 seconds. What is its final velocity?
A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its path, its acceleration is:
quiz.e: Gravity acts continuously; acceleration is always −g (downward) even at the peak where velocity is momentarily zero.

quiz.q: An object starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² for 4 seconds. How far does it travel?
A projectile is launched horizontally from a cliff. Compared to an object simply dropped from the same height at the same time, the projectile:
o: Hits the ground at the same time
quiz.e: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent; both objects have the same initial vertical velocity (0) and the same vertical acceleration (g), so they fall for the same amount of time.

quiz.q: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. What is its initial vertical velocity component?
For maximum range on level ground (no air resistance), a projectile should be launched at an angle of:
quiz.e: Range is maximized at 45° for equal launch and landing heights, ignoring air resistance.

quiz.q: Which of the following can be true for an object with zero velocity?
o: It must be at its starting position
quiz.e: An object can be momentarily at rest while still accelerating, such as a ball at the top of its toss, or a car just starting to move.

quiz.q: A car's velocity-time graph is a horizontal line above the time axis. This means the car has:
quiz.e: A horizontal (flat) line on a v-t graph means velocity isn't changing — constant velocity, zero acceleration.

quiz.q: An object's average speed over a trip is 20 m/s. Its average velocity for the same trip:
o: Could be less than 20 m/s in magnitude
quiz.e: Average speed = total distance/time; average velocity = displacement/time. Since distance ≥ |displacement|, average speed ≥ |average velocity|.

quiz.q: A ball is dropped from rest and falls for 2.0 s. How far does it fall (use g=9.8 m/s²)?
Which kinematic equation should be used if you know vi, a, and $Δx$, and want to find vf without knowing t?
quiz.e: vf² = vi² $+ 2aΔx$ is the only kinematic equation that omits time.

quiz.q: An object moves at constant velocity. What can you conclude about the net force acting on it?
o: It must equal the object's weight
quiz.e: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Newton's Second Law, the net force must be zero.

quiz.q: A 10 kg object experiences a net force of 25 N. What is its acceleration?
Which pair of forces is an example of a Newton's Third Law force pair?
o: Weight and normal force on the same object
The force of a hammer on a nail, and the nail on the hammer
Tension in a rope and gravity on a hanging object
Friction and applied force on the same object
quiz.e: Action-reaction pairs act on two DIFFERENT objects — the hammer pushes the nail, the nail pushes back on the hammer with equal and opposite force.

quiz.q: A book rests on a table. The normal force on the book is equal in magnitude to the book's weight. This is an example of:
o: Two forces on the same object that happen to balance (equilibrium)
quiz.e: Weight and normal force act on the SAME object (the book) and happen to balance since the book isn't accelerating vertically — NOT a third-law pair, which would require different objects.

quiz.q: What is the weight of a 5 kg mass on Earth (g = 9.8 m/s²)?
A box on a horizontal surface has a mass of 8 kg and a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.3. What is the kinetic friction force (g=9.8 m/s²)?
Which statement about mass and weight is correct?
o: Mass and weight are the same thing measured in different units
Mass is constant everywhere; weight depends on local gravity
Weight is constant everywhere; mass depends on local gravity
Both mass and weight change with location
quiz.e: Mass (kg) measures the amount of matter and doesn't change; weight (N) = mg depends on the local gravitational field.

quiz.q: A rope holds a 12 kg mass stationary, hanging vertically. What is the tension in the rope (g=9.8 m/s²)?
quiz.e: Since the mass is in equilibrium, tension equals weight: T = mg = (12)(9.8) = 117.6 N.

quiz.q: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. On the Moon, where gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's, the astronaut's mass is:
o: Zero, since there's no gravity in space
quiz.e: Mass does not change with location — only weight changes. The astronaut's mass remains 70 kg on the Moon.

quiz.q: Which of the following increases the maximum static friction force between two surfaces?
quiz.e: Maximum static friction $fs,max = μsFN$ depends on the normal force (and $μ$), not on contact area or velocity.

quiz.q: A block sits on a frictionless incline at angle $θ$. The component of gravity acting parallel to the incline surface (down the slope) is:
quiz.e: The component of weight parallel to the incline is mg $\sinθ$; the component perpendicular (balanced by normal force) is mg $\cosθ$.

quiz.q: Two blocks are connected by a rope over a frictionless pulley. Which law explains why the same magnitude of acceleration applies to both blocks?
o: The rope is inextensible, constraining both blocks to move together
quiz.e: Because the rope doesn't stretch, both blocks must have the same speed and acceleration magnitude at all times — a constraint, not directly a Newton's law statement.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Newton's Laws of Motion?
o: An object in motion stays in motion unless acted on by a net force
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
Energy cannot be created or destroyed
quiz.e: 'Energy cannot be created or destroyed' is the law of conservation of energy, not one of Newton's three laws of motion.

quiz.q: A 1000 kg car accelerates at 2 m/s². What net force is required?
When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force. This is best explained by:
quiz.e: Newton's Third Law: for every action force, there's an equal and opposite reaction force.

quiz.q: An object is in equilibrium on an incline, held by a rope parallel to the incline. The tension in the rope is:
quiz.e: For equilibrium along the incline, tension must balance the component of gravity along the incline: T = mg $\sinθ$.

quiz.q: Which best describes inertia?
o: The force that keeps objects moving
A property that measures the amount of gravitational force on an object
The tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of motion
The rate of change of momentum
quiz.e: Inertia is the tendency of matter to resist changes in velocity (both magnitude and direction); mass is the quantitative measure of inertia.

quiz.q: A 2 kg object moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
A 3 kg object experiences a net force of 6 N for 2 seconds. What is the impulse delivered?
Airbags reduce injury in car crashes primarily by:
o: Reducing the change in momentum during the crash
Increasing the time over which momentum changes, reducing the force
Increasing the force on the passenger
quiz.e: For a fixed impulse $(Δp)$, extending the time of impact reduces the average force $(J=FΔt)$, which is how airbags reduce injury.

quiz.q: Two objects of equal mass moving in opposite directions with equal speed collide and stick together. What is their final velocity?
quiz.e: Total initial momentum = mv + m(−v) = 0, so by conservation of momentum, final momentum must also be zero, meaning they stop.

quiz.q: Which type of collision conserves both momentum AND kinetic energy?
o: Any collision involving a large object
quiz.e: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and total kinetic energy; inelastic collisions conserve only momentum.

quiz.q: A 4 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides and sticks with a stationary 2 kg cart. What is their common final velocity?
quiz.e: Conservation of momentum: (4)(3) + (2)(0) = (4+2)v → 12 = 6v → v = 2 m/s.

quiz.q: How much work is done by a 10 N force pushing an object 5 m in the direction of the force?
A person carries a heavy bag horizontally at constant velocity across a room. How much work does the person do on the bag (ignoring the initial lift)?
o: Depends on the bag's weight only
quiz.e: The applied force (upward, to support the bag) is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so W = Fd cos90° = 0.

quiz.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 6 m/s?
If the speed of an object doubles, its kinetic energy:
quiz.e: KE ∝ v², so doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.

quiz.q: A 5 kg object is raised 3 m above the ground. What is its gravitational potential energy relative to the ground (g=9.8 m/s²)?
A roller coaster car at the top of a hill has PE = 5000 J and KE = 0 (ignoring friction). What is its KE at the bottom of the hill if PE there is 0?
quiz.e: By conservation of mechanical energy, total energy stays constant: KEf = PEi − PEf + KEi = 5000 − 0 + 0 = 5000 J.

quiz.q: In a real roller coaster with friction, the total mechanical energy at the bottom of a hill compared to the top is:
o: Less, because some energy converts to heat/sound
quiz.e: Friction is a non-conservative force that removes mechanical energy from the system, converting it to heat and sound — total energy (including heat) is still conserved, but mechanical energy decreases.

quiz.q: Which quantity is conserved in ALL collisions, whether elastic or inelastic (assuming an isolated system)?
quiz.e: Momentum is always conserved in an isolated system's collisions; kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.

quiz.q: A spring with spring constant k=200 N/m is compressed 0.1 m. What is the elastic potential energy stored?
A car travels in a circle at constant speed. Which statement is true?
o: The car has zero acceleration since speed is constant
The car has acceleration directed toward the center of the circle
The car has acceleration directed away from the center
quiz.e: Even at constant speed, direction is continuously changing, producing centripetal acceleration directed toward the center.

quiz.q: A 1200 kg car rounds a curve of radius 50 m at 10 m/s. What centripetal force is required?
What force provides the centripetal force for a satellite orbiting Earth?
quiz.e: Gravity between the satellite and Earth supplies the necessary centripetal force for circular orbit.

quiz.q: If the distance between two masses is tripled, the gravitational force between them:
quiz.e: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: Fg ∝ 1/r². Tripling r reduces force to 1/3² = 1/9.

quiz.q: Two masses are doubled (both m1 and m2 double) while distance stays the same. The gravitational force between them becomes:
quiz.e: Fg ∝ m1m2, so doubling both masses multiplies the force by 2×2=4.

quiz.q: A ball on a string is swung in a horizontal circle. What provides the centripetal force?
quiz.e: Tension in the string pulls the ball toward the center, providing the centripetal force.

quiz.q: According to Kepler's Third Law, if planet A orbits at twice the radius of planet B (same central star), planet A's orbital period compared to planet B's is:
An object moves in a circle at constant speed. Which of the following is constant?
o: Centripetal acceleration direction only relative to a fixed axis
quiz.e: Speed (magnitude of velocity) stays constant in uniform circular motion, but velocity direction and acceleration direction continuously change (though acceleration magnitude is constant, its direction always points to the center, which itself is a changing direction in space).

quiz.q: Universal gravitation constant G has units of:
quiz.e: From Fg = Gm1m2/r², G must have units of N·m²/kg² so the equation balances dimensionally.

quiz.q: A satellite orbits at a larger radius than another satellite around the same planet. Compared to the closer satellite, the farther one has:
o: An orbital speed independent of radius
quiz.e: Orbital speed $v=√(Gm/r)$ decreases as r increases — farther satellites move slower.

quiz.q: Why is there no real outward force acting on a passenger in a car turning a corner (in an inertial frame)?
o: Because the passenger's inertia makes them tend to continue in a straight line, while the car curves under them
There actually IS a real outward force, called centrifugal force
quiz.e: In an inertial reference frame, only a real inward (centripetal) net force acts; the sensation of being 'thrown outward' is simply the passenger's inertia resisting the change in direction.

quiz.q: A 500 kg satellite and a 1000 kg satellite orbit Earth at the same radius. Which has the greater orbital speed?
o: Both have the same orbital speed
quiz.e: Orbital speed $v=√(GMEarth/r)$ does not depend on the orbiting satellite's own mass — both have the same speed at the same radius.

quiz.q: Kepler's Second Law states that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. This implies the planet moves:
o: Fastest when farthest from the Sun
Fastest when closest to the Sun
At constant speed throughout its orbit
quiz.e: To sweep equal areas in equal times while closer to the Sun (a shorter radius arm), the planet must move faster near perihelion.

quiz.q: What is the centripetal acceleration of an object moving at 4 m/s in a circle of radius 2 m?
A planet's orbit is best described by Kepler's First Law as:
o: A perfect circle centered on the Sun
An ellipse with the Sun at one focus
quiz.e: Kepler's First Law: planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one of the two foci.

quiz.q: If Earth's radius suddenly doubled with mass unchanged, the gravitational force on an object at the new surface would be:
quiz.e: Fg ∝ 1/r²; doubling the radius (distance to center) reduces surface gravity to 1/4.

quiz.q: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
If the frequency of a wave increases while it stays in the same medium, its wavelength:
quiz.e: Since $v=fλ$ and speed is fixed by the medium, increasing f must decrease $λ$ proportionally.

quiz.q: Sound is best classified as a:
quiz.e: Sound is a longitudinal wave — particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave travel, creating compressions and rarefactions.

quiz.q: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because:
o: Sound waves are too weak in a vacuum
Sound requires a medium (particles) to compress and rarefy
The vacuum absorbs all sound energy
Light waves interfere with sound in a vacuum
quiz.e: Sound is a mechanical wave requiring particles to transmit compressions and rarefactions; a vacuum has no particles.

quiz.q: Sound travels fastest through which medium?
quiz.e: Sound travels fastest in solids because particles are closest together and transmit vibrations most efficiently, slower in liquids, slowest in gases.

quiz.q: Two identical waves arrive perfectly in phase at the same point. This is an example of:
quiz.e: In-phase waves add their displacements together, producing a larger amplitude — constructive interference.

quiz.q: An ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched as it approaches you and lower-pitched as it drives away. This is:
quiz.e: The Doppler effect: the source moving toward you compresses wavefronts (higher perceived frequency); moving away stretches them (lower perceived frequency).

quiz.q: What actually happens to the siren's emitted frequency as the ambulance moves toward and then away from a stationary observer?
o: It stays exactly the same the whole time — only the perceived frequency changes
quiz.e: The source's actual emitted frequency never changes; only the frequency perceived by the observer shifts due to relative motion.

quiz.q: Which best describes amplitude?
o: The number of cycles per second
The maximum displacement from equilibrium, related to a wave's energy
quiz.e: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium and relates to the energy/intensity (loudness for sound) carried by the wave.

quiz.q: A standing wave is formed by:
o: A single wave traveling in one direction
Two identical waves traveling in opposite directions in a confined medium
quiz.e: Standing waves result from the superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions, creating fixed nodes and antinodes.

quiz.q: A wave's period is 0.25 s. What is its frequency?
Which property of a sound wave corresponds to its perceived pitch?
quiz.e: Pitch corresponds directly to frequency — higher frequency sounds are perceived as higher pitch.

quiz.q: Points of maximum displacement in a standing wave are called:
quiz.e: Antinodes are points of maximum displacement; nodes are points of zero displacement.

quiz.q: Resonance occurs when:
o: A wave completely destructively interferes with itself
A system is driven at its natural frequency, producing a large amplitude increase
Two waves travel through each other unaffected
A wave reflects off a fixed boundary
quiz.e: Resonance is a dramatic amplitude increase that occurs when a driving frequency matches a system's natural frequency.

quiz.q: A wave's amplitude is doubled. Its wave speed:
o: Stays the same, since speed depends on the medium
quiz.e: Wave speed depends only on the properties of the medium, not amplitude or frequency.

quiz.q: Two point charges of $+2 μC$ and $+3 μC$ are separated by 0.1 m. What is the electric force between them (k=8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C²)?
If the distance between two charges is halved, the electric force between them becomes:
quiz.e: Coulomb's law is inverse-square: halving r increases force by a factor of (1/0.5)²=4.

quiz.q: Electric field lines around an isolated positive charge point:
quiz.e: Field lines point away from positive charges (the direction a positive test charge would be pushed) and toward negative charges.

quiz.q: A resistor has V=12 V across it and carries I=3 A. What is its resistance?
Three $2 Ω$ resistors are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
quiz.e: Series resistances add directly: Rtotal = $2+2+2 = 6 Ω$.

quiz.q: Three $6 Ω$ resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
In a series circuit with two resistors, which quantity is the same through both resistors?
quiz.e: In a series circuit, there's only one path, so the current is identical through every component.

quiz.q: In a parallel circuit, which quantity is the same across every branch?
quiz.e: Each parallel branch connects across the same two nodes, so voltage is identical across all branches.

quiz.q: A circuit has a 12 V source and total resistance of $4 Ω$. What is the total current?
A device draws 2 A at 120 V. What power does it consume?
If one bulb burns out (opens) in a series string of holiday lights, what happens to the rest of the string?
o: The rest also go out, since the circuit is broken
quiz.e: In a series circuit there's only one current path; if it's broken anywhere, no current flows anywhere in the loop.

quiz.q: If one branch fails (opens) in a parallel circuit, what happens to the other branches?
quiz.e: Parallel branches are independent paths; if one opens, current can still flow through the remaining branches.

quiz.q: Which of the following increases the resistance of a wire?
quiz.e: R = ρL/A — resistance increases directly with length and decreases with cross-sectional area.

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
quiz.e: The coulomb (C) is the SI unit of electric charge.

quiz.q: A charge of 4 C flows past a point in a wire in 2 seconds. What is the current?
Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor does what to the power dissipated?
quiz.e: P = V²/R, so doubling V quadruples P (for constant R).

quiz.q: Which statement about magnetic poles is correct?
o: Isolated magnetic monopoles have been observed in labs
Like poles attract and opposite poles repel
Like poles repel and opposite poles attract
Magnets only have a single pole
quiz.e: As with electric charges, like magnetic poles repel and opposite poles attract; monopoles have never been observed.

quiz.q: Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines point:
quiz.e: Outside the magnet, field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole, forming closed loops through the magnet's interior.

quiz.q: A charged particle moves parallel to a magnetic field. What magnetic force does it experience?
o: Force perpendicular to both v and B, of medium size
quiz.e: F = qvB $\sinθ$; when $θ=0°$ (parallel), $\sinθ=0$, so the force is zero.

quiz.q: A charged particle moves perpendicular to a magnetic field. What is the shape of its resulting path?
quiz.e: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, continuously changing direction without changing speed — producing uniform circular motion.

quiz.q: The magnetic force on a moving charge does what to its kinetic energy?
o: Leaves it unchanged, since the force is always perpendicular to velocity
quiz.e: Since F is always perpendicular to v, it does no work on the charge, so kinetic energy (and speed) stays constant.

quiz.q: What is required to induce an EMF in a loop of wire via electromagnetic induction?
o: A strong, constant magnetic field through the loop
A changing magnetic flux through the loop
A stationary magnet near the loop
Any magnetic field, changing or not
quiz.e: Faraday's Law requires a CHANGING magnetic flux — a constant field through a stationary loop induces nothing.

quiz.q: According to Lenz's Law, an induced current flows in a direction that:
o: Increases the change in flux that caused it
Opposes the change in flux that caused it
Has no relationship to the change in flux
quiz.e: Lenz's Law: induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux, consistent with conservation of energy.

quiz.q: A generator converts:
quiz.e: A generator uses mechanical motion (rotating a coil in a magnetic field) to induce an EMF — converting mechanical to electrical energy.

quiz.q: A motor converts:
quiz.e: A motor uses current in a magnetic field to produce a force (torque), converting electrical energy into mechanical motion.

quiz.q: A wire carrying current I=5 A, of length 0.4 m, sits perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.2 T. What force does it experience?
Increasing the number of turns in a coil used for electromagnetic induction:
o: Has no effect on the induced EMF
quiz.e: More turns means the changing flux links more loops, increasing the total induced EMF.

quiz.q: The direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire is found using:
quiz.e: The right-hand rule: point the thumb along conventional current, and the curled fingers show the direction of the circular magnetic field.

quiz.q: A magnet is pushed into a stationary coil of wire, inducing a current. If the magnet is pushed in faster, the induced EMF:
quiz.e: Faster motion means a faster rate of change of flux, which increases the induced EMF (Faraday's Law).

quiz.q: Why do AC generators produce alternating (rather than direct) current?
o: Because the coil's orientation relative to the magnetic field continuously changes as it rotates
Because the magnetic field alternates on its own
quiz.e: As the coil rotates, the rate and direction of flux change through it varies sinusoidally, producing an alternating induced EMF.

quiz.q: Which of the following experiences zero magnetic force in a magnetic field?
o: A charge moving perpendicular to the field
A charge moving at an angle to the field
A current-carrying wire perpendicular to the field
quiz.e: Magnetic force depends on velocity $(F=qvB \sinθ)$; a stationary charge (v=0) experiences no magnetic force.

quiz.q: A light ray strikes a plane mirror at 30° from the normal. At what angle does it reflect?
quiz.e: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal, so it reflects at 30° from the normal.

quiz.q: A plane mirror image is:
o: Virtual, upright, same size as the object
quiz.e: A flat (plane) mirror always forms a virtual, upright, same-size image located as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

quiz.q: Light travels from air (n=1.00) into glass (n=1.50). It will bend:
quiz.e: Light bends toward the normal when entering a medium with a higher index of refraction (denser, slower light speed).

quiz.q: Light in water (n=1.33) hits the water-air boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle. What happens?
o: It refracts into the air as normal
Total internal reflection occurs — all light reflects back into the water
The light splits into a rainbow
quiz.e: Beyond the critical angle, going from a denser to less dense medium, total internal reflection occurs — no light exits.

quiz.q: Using Snell's Law, light passes from a medium with n1=1.5 into a medium with n2=1.0, hitting the boundary at 30° from the normal. Which best describes the refracted angle?
o: Less than 30°, bending toward the normal
Greater than 30°, bending away from the normal
quiz.e: $n1sinθ1=n2sinθ2$ → since n2<n1, $\sinθ2$ must be larger than $\sinθ1$, so $θ2>30°$ — light bends away from the normal entering a less dense medium.

quiz.q: A convex (converging) lens forms what kind of image when the object is placed beyond the focal point?
quiz.e: When do>f for a converging lens, light rays converge on the far side, forming a real, inverted image.

quiz.q: An object is placed inside the focal length of a convex lens (do<f). The resulting image is:
quiz.e: When the object is closer than the focal point, the lens acts as a magnifying glass, producing a virtual, upright, magnified image.

quiz.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex lens with a focal length of 10 cm. Using 1/f=1/do+1/di, what is the image distance?
A convex mirror (like a car's passenger side mirror) always forms an image that is:
quiz.e: Convex (diverging) mirrors always produce virtual, upright, reduced images, giving a wider field of view.

quiz.q: Which type of lens or mirror can form a REAL image?
o: Concave (converging) mirror, if the object is beyond the focal point
Any lens or mirror, regardless of type
quiz.e: Only converging elements (convex lens, concave mirror) can produce real images, and only when the object is beyond the focal point.

quiz.q: What is the index of refraction of a medium in which light travels at 2.0×10⁸ m/s (c=3.0×10⁸ m/s)?
Which best explains why a straw appears bent at the water's surface when viewed from the side?
o: Refraction — light bends as it passes from water into air
quiz.e: Refraction bends light rays as they cross the water-air boundary due to the change in speed, making the submerged part of the straw appear displaced/bent.

quiz.q: A magnification of m=−2 for an image means:
o: The image is upright and twice the size
The image is inverted and twice the size
The image is upright and half the size
The image is inverted and half the size
quiz.e: A negative m indicates an inverted image; the magnitude (2) means the image is twice the height of the object.

quiz.q: Diffuse reflection occurs because:
o: The surface is rough, scattering parallel rays in many directions
The angle of incidence is zero
quiz.e: A rough surface reflects parallel incoming rays at many different angles (still following the law of reflection at each microscopic point), preventing a clear image from forming.

quiz.q: The critical angle for total internal reflection depends on:
o: The ratio of the two media's indices of refraction
quiz.e: $\sinθc = n2/n1$, so the critical angle depends on the ratio of the refractive indices of the two media.

quiz.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency mainly increases:
o: The maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons
The work function of the metal
quiz.e: Intensity relates to the number of photons hitting the metal per second, which increases the number (rate) of ejected electrons, not their individual energy.

quiz.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the frequency of light (above threshold) mainly increases:
o: The maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons
quiz.e: Each photon's energy is E=hf; higher frequency means each photon carries more energy, increasing the max KE of ejected electrons (KEmax=hf−W0).

quiz.q: A metal has a work function of 2.0 eV. Light with photon energy 3.0 eV strikes it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron?
Light striking a metal below its threshold frequency, no matter how intense, will:
o: Eject electrons with high kinetic energy
Eject many electrons but with low kinetic energy
Eject electrons only after a time delay
quiz.e: Below the threshold frequency, individual photons don't carry enough energy to overcome the work function, so no electrons are ejected regardless of intensity.

quiz.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle is given by:
quiz.e: De Broglie's relation: $λ = h/p = h/(mv)$, describing the wave nature of matter.

quiz.q: Which experiment provides strong evidence for the wave nature of light?
quiz.e: Double-slit diffraction and interference patterns are classic evidence of light's wave nature; the photoelectric effect instead evidences light's particle nature.

quiz.q: In the Bohr model, an atom emits a photon when:
o: An electron absorbs energy and jumps to a higher level
An electron falls from a higher to a lower energy level
quiz.e: A photon is emitted when an electron transitions from a higher to a lower allowed energy level, releasing energy equal to the level difference.

quiz.q: Bright-line emission spectra are unique to each element because:
o: Each element has the exact same energy levels
Each element has its own unique set of quantized electron energy levels
Bright-line spectra are actually identical for all elements
Emission spectra depend only on temperature
quiz.e: Each element has a distinct set of quantized energy levels, so the photon energies (and thus wavelengths) it can emit/absorb form a unique 'fingerprint.'

quiz.q: Which particle is emitted in alpha decay?
quiz.e: Alpha decay emits an alpha particle, which is a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons).

quiz.q: After an alpha decay, the mass number and atomic number of the parent nucleus change by:
quiz.e: Alpha decay removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2.

quiz.q: Which type of radioactive decay is stopped by just a sheet of paper?
quiz.e: Alpha particles have the least penetrating power (but highest ionizing power) and are stopped by paper or skin.

quiz.q: Which type of radioactive decay requires lead or thick concrete to stop?
quiz.e: Gamma rays are high-energy photons with the greatest penetrating power, requiring dense shielding like lead or thick concrete.

quiz.q: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 4 days. After 12 days, what fraction of the original sample remains?
quiz.e: 12 days = 3 half-lives, so the remaining fraction is (1/2)³ = 1/8.

quiz.q: Nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun, involves:
o: Splitting a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei
Combining light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
Emitting only gamma rays with no nuclear change
Converting an electron into a proton
quiz.e: Fusion combines light nuclei (e.g., hydrogen into helium), releasing a large amount of energy — the process that powers stars.

quiz.q: According to mass-energy equivalence, a small amount of mass converted entirely to energy releases:
o: An amount of energy given by E=mc², which is very large due to c²
Energy only in the form of heat
No energy; mass and energy are unrelated
quiz.e: E=mc² shows that even a tiny mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy because c² (≈9×10¹⁶ m²/s²) is such a large number.

quiz.q: Beta decay involves:
o: A neutron converting to a proton (or vice versa), emitting an electron or positron
Emission of a high-energy photon with no change in atomic number
Splitting of the nucleus into two roughly equal parts
quiz.e: In beta-minus decay, a neutron converts to a proton and an electron (beta particle) is emitted; atomic number increases by 1, mass number stays the same.

quiz.q: A car speeds up from 12 m/s to 30 m/s in 6.0 s. What is its acceleration?
Starting from rest, an object accelerates $at 4.0 m/s^2$ for 5.0 s. How far does it travel?
A ball is dropped from rest. How fast is it moving after $3.0 s (g = 9.8 m/s^2)?$
A runner jogs 300 m east, then 100 m west. What is the magnitude of the displacement?
quiz.e: 300 east - 100 west = 200 m east; distance would be 400 m.

quiz.q: On a velocity-time graph, what does the slope of the line represent?
quiz.e: The slope of a v-t graph is the rate of change of velocity, i.e. acceleration.

quiz.q: A stone is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. Approximately how long until it returns to the thrower's hand $(g = 10 m/s^2)?$
quiz.e: Time up = 20/10 = 2 s; total flight is symmetric, so about 4 s.

quiz.q: A projectile is launched horizontally at 15 m/s from a 20 m cliff $(g = 10 m/s^2)$. How long is it in the air?
quiz.e: $20 = 0.5(10)t^2$ gives $t^2 = 4, t = 2.0 s$; horizontal speed does not affect fall time.

quiz.q: For that same projectile (15 m/s horizontal, 2.0 s aloft), how far from the base of the cliff does it land?
quiz.e: Range = $v_x t = 15 x 2.0 = 30 m$.

quiz.q: A car moving at 25 m/s brakes to a stop over 50 m. What is its acceleration?
At the highest point of its path, a ball thrown straight up has:
o: zero velocity and downward acceleration g
quiz.e: Vertical velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still acts, so acceleration is g downward.

quiz.q: Which launch angle gives the maximum range for a projectile on level ground (no air resistance)?
quiz.e: Range is proportional to sin(2theta), which is largest at theta = 45 degrees.

quiz.q: Distance traveled is always:
o: greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement
quiz.e: Distance is the total path length and can never be less than the straight-line displacement magnitude.

quiz.q: An astronaut drops a hammer from 2.0 m above the Moon's surface, where g = 1.62 m/s². How long does it take to reach the surface?
quiz.e: Starting from rest, d = ½gt², so t = √(2d ÷ g) = √(4.0 ÷ 1.62) = √2.47 ≈ 1.6 s.

quiz.q: A coin and a feather are dropped together inside a tube with the air pumped out. They:
o: hit the bottom at the same time
fall so the coin lands first
fall so the feather lands first
float, because there is no gravity in a vacuum
quiz.e: Without air resistance, gravity gives every object the same acceleration, so they fall together. Gravity still acts in a vacuum.

quiz.q: Who taught that heavier objects fall faster, in proportion to their weight?
quiz.e: Aristotle held that view. Galileo later showed that, apart from air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration.

quiz.q: An object is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), its speed after 2.0 s is about:
quiz.e: v = gt = (9.8)(2.0) = 19.6 ≈ 20 m/s. Each second of free fall adds 9.8 m/s.

quiz.q: In a reaction-time test, a ruler falls 0.20 m before a student catches it. The student's reaction time is about (g = 9.8 m/s²):
quiz.e: From rest, t = √(2d/g) = √(2 × 0.20 ÷ 9.8) = √0.041 ≈ 0.20 s. 0.041 forgets the square root.

quiz.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its flight, its velocity and acceleration are:
quiz.e: The ball stops for an instant, but gravity never switches off, so the acceleration is still g downward.

quiz.q: A rock is dropped from rest off a 20. m ledge. Ignoring air resistance (g = 9.8 m/s²), it reaches the ground in about:
quiz.e: t = √(2d/g) = √(40. ÷ 9.8) = √4.1 ≈ 2.0 s. 4.1 s forgets the square root.

quiz.q: A ball is thrown straight up at 15 m/s (g = 9.8 m/s²). How long does it take to reach the top?
quiz.e: At the top v = 0, so 0 = 15 − 9.8t and t = 15 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 1.5 s. 3.1 s is the whole trip up and back down.

quiz.q: A 5.0 kg block is pushed with a net force of 20 N. What is its acceleration?
What is the weight of a 12 kg object near Earth's surface $(g = 9.8 m/s^2)?$
An object moves at constant velocity. The net force on it is:
quiz.e: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero (equilibrium).

quiz.q: A book rests on a table. The reaction partner (Newton's third law) to Earth's gravitational pull on the book is:
o: the table's normal force on the book
the book's gravitational pull on Earth
quiz.e: The action-reaction partner of Earth pulling the book is the book pulling Earth with equal, opposite force.

quiz.q: A 2.0 kg box on a level floor has $mu_k = 0.30$. What is the kinetic friction force while it slides $(g = 10 m/s^2)?$
On a frictionless incline at 30 degrees, the acceleration of a sliding block is $(g = 10 m/s^2)$:
Doubling the net force on an object while keeping its mass the same will:
quiz.e: a is proportional to $F_{net}$, so doubling the force doubles the acceleration.

quiz.q: The normal force on a book lying on a horizontal table (no other vertical forces) equals:
quiz.e: With no vertical acceleration, the upward normal force balances the downward weight.

quiz.q: Which statement about mass and weight is correct?
o: Mass changes on the Moon; weight does not
Weight changes with location; mass does not
quiz.e: Mass is an amount of matter (constant); weight = mg depends on local g.

quiz.q: A 10 N horizontal force is applied to a 4.0 kg box, and friction is 2.0 N. The acceleration is:
Static friction acting on a stationary crate that no one is pushing is:
quiz.e: Static friction only acts to oppose an applied force or tendency to slide; with no push it is zero.

quiz.q: A tension of 40 N supports a hanging mass at rest. The mass is $(g = 10 m/s^2)$:
How much work is done lifting a 20 N object 3.0 m straight up at constant speed?
A 2.0 kg object moves at 4.0 m/s. Its kinetic energy is:
A force perpendicular to an object's displacement does how much work?
quiz.e: W = Fd cos(90) = 0.

quiz.q: A 1.0 kg ball is dropped from 5.0 m. Its speed just before landing is ($g = 10 m/s^2$, no air resistance):
quiz.e: mgh = $0.5 m v^2$ gives v = sqrt(2 x 10 x 5.0) = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: A motor does 6000 J of work in 30 s. Its power output is:
The momentum of a 3.0 kg cart moving at 2.0 m/s is:
A 0.10 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m/s and bounces straight back at 6.0 m/s. The magnitude of the impulse on the ball is:
Two objects stick together after colliding. This collision is:
quiz.e: Objects moving off with a common velocity define a perfectly inelastic collision.

quiz.q: In every collision in an isolated system, which quantity is always conserved?
quiz.e: Total momentum is conserved in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.

quiz.q: A car's speed doubles. Its kinetic energy becomes:
quiz.e: KE is proportional to $v^2$, so doubling v quadruples KE.

quiz.q: A 500 N force pushes a crate 4.0 m across a floor. If 300 J is lost to friction, the crate's kinetic energy increases by:
Airbags reduce injury in a crash mainly because they:
o: increase the collision time, lowering the peak force
increase the force on the passenger
quiz.e: For a fixed change in momentum, a longer contact time means a smaller average force.

quiz.q: A 60 kg skater at rest throws a 2.0 kg ball east at 9.0 m/s. The skater's recoil speed is about:
Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is calculated as:
quiz.e: $PE_{gravity} =$ mgh, measured from a chosen reference height.

quiz.q: A motorcycle helmet has impact-absorbing foam under a rigid shell. Which design change best reduces impact-force injuries to the rider's head?
o: Increase the foam thickness to increase the time over which the impact force acts
Decrease the foam thickness to decrease the time over which the impact force acts
Decrease the foam thickness to increase the head's change in speed
Increase the foam thickness to decrease the head's change in speed
quiz.e: Impulse: FΔt = mΔv. The crash fixes the head's change in momentum, so stretching the stopping time Δt lowers the average force F. Thicker foam takes longer to compress.

quiz.q: From 2000 to 2020 the efficiency of U.S. natural-gas power plants rose from about 30% to about 43%. Which statement is correct?
o: The ratio of energy output to energy input increased
The energy output became greater than the energy input
The energy input and output increased by the same proportion
Less energy was wasted as heat because more fuel was burned
quiz.e: Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ energy input. A higher efficiency means a larger output-to-input ratio; output can never exceed input.

quiz.q: A 0.50 kg ball on a 1.0 m string moves in a circle at 4.0 m/s. The centripetal acceleration is:
For that ball (0.50 kg, $a_c = 16 m/s^2$), the required centripetal force is:
Centripetal acceleration always points:
o: toward the center of the circle
quiz.e: It is the acceleration that continually turns the velocity toward the center.

quiz.q: If the distance between two masses triples, the gravitational force between them becomes:
quiz.e: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: force is proportional to $1/r^2$.

quiz.q: An astronaut feels weightless in an orbiting station because:
o: there is no gravity that far from Earth
the station and astronaut are in free fall together
the station spins fast enough to cancel gravity
quiz.e: Both fall toward Earth with the same acceleration, so there is no normal force between them.

quiz.q: The force that keeps a car moving around a flat, level curve is:
o: static friction between tires and road
quiz.e: Static friction points toward the center of the curve and supplies the centripetal force.

quiz.q: Surface gravitational field strength is g = 9.8 N/kg. This is numerically equal to:
quiz.e: N/kg and $m/s^2$ are equivalent units; both describe the free-fall acceleration.

quiz.q: For satellites orbiting Earth, a larger orbital radius corresponds to:
quiz.e: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, so speed decreases as r increases.

quiz.q: At the top of a vertical circular loop, the forces providing the centripetal force on a car are:
o: gravity plus the normal force (both point down toward the center)
quiz.e: At the top, both weight and the track's normal force point downward, toward the center.

quiz.q: Doubling the speed of an object in uniform circular motion (same radius) changes the centripetal force by a factor of:
quiz.e: $F_c$ is proportional to $v^2$, so doubling v quadruples the force.

quiz.q: Weight differs on the Moon compared with Earth because:
o: the gravitational field strength g is different
quiz.e: Weight = mg, and the Moon's surface g is about 1/6 of Earth's.

quiz.q: The period of an object in uniform circular motion is the time to:
quiz.e: Period T is the time for one complete trip around the circle.

quiz.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4.0 m. Its speed is:
quiz.e: v = f lambda = 50 x 4.0 = 200 m/s.

quiz.q: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium move:
o: parallel to the wave's direction of travel
perpendicular to the wave's direction of travel
in the same direction as the energy, then back
quiz.e: Transverse means particle displacement is perpendicular to wave propagation.

quiz.q: Sound is an example of which type of wave?
quiz.e: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave; particle motion is parallel to propagation.

quiz.q: When a wave passes from one medium into another, the quantity that stays the same is:
quiz.e: Frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction; speed and wavelength do.

quiz.q: A police siren sounds higher in pitch as the car approaches you. This is:
quiz.e: Approaching motion compresses the wavefronts, raising the observed frequency.

quiz.q: Two sound waves of 256 Hz and 260 Hz are played together. The beat frequency is:
quiz.e: Beat frequency is the difference: |260 - 256| = 4 Hz.

quiz.q: At a node of a standing wave, the medium:
quiz.e: A node is a point of zero displacement; antinodes have maximum amplitude.

quiz.q: The speed of a wave on a string depends mainly on:
o: the properties of the string (tension and mass per length)
quiz.e: Wave speed is a property of the medium; changing frequency changes wavelength, not speed.

quiz.q: Increasing the frequency of a wave in a fixed medium causes its wavelength to:
quiz.e: Since v = f lambda and v is fixed, higher f means shorter lambda.

quiz.q: Sound cannot travel through:
quiz.e: A mechanical wave like sound needs a medium; a vacuum has none.

quiz.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode. The string length equals:
quiz.e: The fundamental fits one half-wavelength between the two fixed ends (nodes).

quiz.q: Loudness of a sound is most directly related to a wave's:
quiz.e: Greater amplitude carries more energy, heard as greater loudness; frequency sets pitch.

quiz.q: Two point charges are separated by a distance r. If r is halved, the electric force between them becomes:
quiz.e: Coulomb's law is inverse-square: halving r multiplies the force by 4.

quiz.q: The electric field points:
o: from negative charges toward positive charges
away from positive charges and toward negative charges
opposite to the force on a positive test charge
quiz.e: By convention E points the way a positive test charge would be pushed: out of + and into -.

quiz.q: A 12 V battery drives 3.0 A through a resistor. The resistance is:
Power dissipated by a resistor carrying 2.0 A with 6.0 V across it is:
Two 6 ohm resistors are connected in series. The total resistance is:
quiz.e: Series resistances add: 6 + 6 = 12 ohms.

quiz.q: Two 6 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. The total resistance is:
In a series circuit, which quantity is the same through every component?
quiz.e: A series circuit has one path, so the current is identical everywhere.

quiz.q: Adding another resistor in parallel to a circuit causes the total resistance to:
quiz.e: Parallel paths give current more ways to flow, lowering total resistance.

quiz.q: Electric current is defined as:
o: voltage per unit resistance times time
quiz.e: I = delta q / delta t, measured in amperes (coulombs per second).

quiz.q: Like electric charges:
quiz.e: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

quiz.q: An ideal voltmeter is connected:
o: in series and has zero resistance
in parallel and has very high resistance
in series and has very high resistance
in parallel and has zero resistance
quiz.e: A voltmeter measures potential difference across a component, so it is in parallel with high resistance to avoid drawing current.

quiz.q: Charging a balloon by rubbing it on hair transfers:
o: protons from the hair to the balloon
quiz.e: Rubbing moves electrons from one surface to the other; total charge is conserved.

quiz.q: The magnetic force on a charged particle moving parallel to a magnetic field is:
quiz.e: F = qvB sin(theta); when v is parallel to B, sin(0) = 0.

quiz.q: A steady magnetic field passes through a stationary wire loop. The induced EMF is:
quiz.e: Induction requires a CHANGING flux; a steady field through a still loop induces nothing.

quiz.q: Lenz's law states that an induced current flows in the direction that:
o: opposes the change in flux that produced it
quiz.e: The induced current opposes the flux change, consistent with energy conservation.

quiz.q: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary than the primary. It:
quiz.e: $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$; ideally power is conserved, so higher voltage means lower current.

quiz.q: Magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire form:
quiz.e: The right-hand rule gives circular field lines encircling the wire.

quiz.q: The magnetic force on a moving charge does no work because it:
quiz.e: A force perpendicular to velocity changes direction but not speed, so it does zero work.

quiz.q: A generator converts:
quiz.e: Rotating a coil in a magnetic field changes flux and induces an EMF.

quiz.q: Two parallel wires carry current in the same direction. They:
quiz.e: Parallel currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel.

quiz.q: Increasing the number of turns per unit length in a solenoid (same current):
quiz.e: Solenoid field strength grows with current and with turns per unit length.

quiz.q: A magnetic flux through a loop can change by:
o: changing B, the loop area, or the loop's orientation
quiz.e: Flux = B A cos(theta); any of B, A, or theta changing alters the flux.

quiz.q: An electromagnet differs from a permanent magnet mainly because it:
o: can be switched on and off
quiz.e: An electromagnet's field exists only while current flows, so it can be turned off.

quiz.q: According to the law of reflection, the angle of incidence is measured from the:
quiz.e: Both incidence and reflection angles are measured from the normal, and they are equal.

quiz.q: A plane mirror forms an image that is:
o: virtual, upright, and the same size
quiz.e: A flat mirror produces a virtual, upright, same-size image as far behind as the object is in front.

quiz.q: Light slows down when it enters a medium with a higher index of refraction and bends:
quiz.e: Going into a slower (denser) medium, the ray bends toward the normal.

quiz.q: The index of refraction of a medium is defined as:
quiz.e: $n = c/v_{medium}$, so a larger n means slower light and n is at least 1.

quiz.q: A converging (convex) lens forms a real, inverted image when the object is:
quiz.e: Objects beyond the focal length of a converging lens produce real, inverted images.

quiz.q: A diverging (concave) lens always forms an image that is:
o: the same size as the object
quiz.e: A diverging lens can only make virtual, upright, smaller images.

quiz.q: Total internal reflection can occur only when light travels from a medium of:
o: high index to low index, beyond the critical angle
quiz.e: TIR requires going toward a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle.

quiz.q: When white light passes through a prism and spreads into colors, this is called:
quiz.e: Dispersion results because the index of refraction varies slightly with wavelength.

quiz.q: All electromagnetic waves in a vacuum travel at:
quiz.e: Every EM wave travels $at c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s$ in vacuum, regardless of frequency.

quiz.q: Which list orders electromagnetic waves from longest to shortest wavelength?
quiz.e: Radio has the longest wavelength; then infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

quiz.q: When light refracts entering water, which property does NOT change?
quiz.e: Frequency (and color) is fixed by the source; speed, wavelength, and direction change.

quiz.q: A double-slit experiment produces alternating bright and dark bands because of:
quiz.e: Light waves from the two slits interfere constructively (bright) and destructively (dark).

quiz.q: The energy of a photon is given by:
quiz.e: Photon energy E = hf = hc/lambda, with h Planck's constant.

quiz.q: In the photoelectric effect, electrons are ejected from a metal only if the light's:
quiz.e: Below the threshold frequency, no electrons are ejected no matter how bright the light.

quiz.q: Increasing the frequency of light above the photoelectric threshold increases the:
o: maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons
quiz.e: $KE_{max} =$ hf - W, so higher f gives each electron more kinetic energy.

quiz.q: An atom emits light of a specific wavelength when an electron:
o: drops from a higher energy level to a lower one
quiz.e: The photon energy equals the difference between the two electron energy levels.

quiz.q: In alpha decay, the atomic number of the nucleus:
quiz.e: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, so the parent loses 2 protons (and 2 neutrons).

quiz.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time for:
o: all of the sample to decay
half of the sample to decay
quiz.e: After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain; it is constant for a given isotope.

quiz.q: $E = mc^2$ tells us that:
o: a small mass corresponds to a large energy
quiz.e: Because $c^2$ is very large, converting a tiny amount of mass releases enormous energy.

quiz.q: Nuclear fusion involves:
o: splitting a heavy nucleus into lighter ones
combining light nuclei into a heavier one
an electron falling to a lower level
a proton turning into a neutron
quiz.e: Fusion joins light nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) and powers the Sun.

quiz.q: A beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a:
quiz.e: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted, raising the atomic number by 1.

quiz.q: Each chemical element produces a unique:
quiz.e: The spacing of an element's energy levels gives it a characteristic set of spectral lines.

quiz.q: Gamma decay changes a nucleus's:
o: energy, but not its atomic or mass number
quiz.e: A gamma ray is a photon; the nucleus loses energy but keeps the same protons and neutrons.

quiz.q: One complete revolution is equal to how many radians?
quiz.e: One full circle is 2 pi radians (equivalently 360 degrees).

quiz.q: Torque is calculated as:
o: force times the perpendicular lever arm
quiz.e: Torque = r F sin(theta), i.e. force times the perpendicular distance to the axis.

quiz.q: A force applied directly through the axis of rotation produces:
quiz.e: The lever arm is zero, so the torque is zero regardless of the force's size.

quiz.q: An object is in rotational equilibrium when:
o: the net torque on it is zero
all forces point toward the axis
quiz.e: Rotational equilibrium requires the sum of torques (and forces) to be zero.

quiz.q: Moment of inertia depends on:
o: the mass and how it is distributed relative to the axis
quiz.e: I depends on each mass element and the square of its distance from the axis.

quiz.q: A skater spinning with arms out pulls them in. Her angular speed:
quiz.e: Pulling in reduces I; with angular momentum conserved, omega increases.

quiz.q: The rotational form of Newton's second law is:
quiz.e: Net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

quiz.q: A door handle is placed far from the hinges because this:
o: increases the torque for a given push
quiz.e: A longer lever arm produces more torque from the same force.

quiz.q: Angular momentum of a rotating body is:
quiz.e: L = I omega; it is conserved when no external torque acts.

quiz.q: A solid sphere and a hoop of equal mass and radius roll down the same ramp from rest. The one reaching the bottom first is:
o: it depends on the ramp color
quiz.e: The sphere has a smaller $I/(MR^2)$, so more of its energy goes into translation; it wins.

quiz.q: A wheel rotating at 3.0 rad/s speeds up uniformly to 9.0 rad/s in 2.0 s. Its angular acceleration is:
All points on a rigid spinning disk share the same:
quiz.e: Every point turns through the same angle in the same time, so omega is common; linear speed grows with radius.

quiz.q: For an object in simple harmonic motion, the restoring force is:
o: proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium
quiz.e: SHM is defined by F = -k x, a restoring force growing with displacement.

quiz.q: The period of a mass on a spring is T = 2 pi $\sqrt{m/k}$. Quadrupling the mass:
quiz.e: T is proportional to sqrt(m), so 4x mass gives 2x period.

quiz.q: The period of a simple pendulum depends on:
quiz.e: T = 2 pi $\sqrt{L/g}$; mass and (small) amplitude do not matter.

quiz.q: A pendulum clock is taken to the Moon, where g is smaller. The clock will:
quiz.e: Smaller g means a longer period, so each swing takes longer and the clock runs slow.

quiz.q: In SHM, the speed of the oscillator is greatest:
quiz.e: All the energy is kinetic at equilibrium, so the speed peaks there.

quiz.q: In SHM, the acceleration has its largest magnitude:
quiz.e: Acceleration is proportional to displacement, so it is largest at the extremes.

quiz.q: Increasing the amplitude of an ideal mass-spring oscillator changes its period:
quiz.e: The period of ideal SHM is independent of amplitude.

quiz.q: The total mechanical energy of a mass-spring system in SHM is:
quiz.e: At the turning point all energy is elastic PE = $0.5 k A^2$, and it stays constant.

quiz.q: Damping in a real oscillator mainly causes the:
quiz.e: Energy loss to friction/air resistance shrinks the amplitude while barely changing the period.

quiz.q: Resonance occurs when a system is driven at:
o: a frequency far from its natural frequency
quiz.e: Driving at a natural frequency transfers energy efficiently and builds a large amplitude.

quiz.q: A 0.50 kg mass on a spring with k = 200 N/m has a period of about:
Quadrupling the length of a simple pendulum changes its period by a factor of:
quiz.e: T is proportional to sqrt(L), so 4x length gives 2x period.

hardQuiz.e: Distance 7.0 km in 35 min = 7.0 / (35/60) = 12 km/h.

hardQuiz.e: 200 cos 30° ≈ 173 N (the parallel component is 200 sin 30° = 100 N).

hardQuiz.q: Forces of 30. N east and 40. N north act on an object. The equilibrant is:
hardQuiz.e: The resultant is 50 N to the northeast, and the equilibrant is equal and opposite.

hardQuiz.q: A 10.0 m displacement at 30° above the +x axis is followed by a 5.0 m displacement along +x. The magnitude of the total displacement is about:

hardQuiz.e: A negative scalar reverses the direction, and the factor 2 doubles the magnitude.

hardQuiz.q: A car covers the first half of a trip at 30 m/s and the second half of the same distance at 60 m/s. Its average speed is:
hardQuiz.e: For distance d each way, t = d/30 + d/60 = d/20, so the average is 2d / (d/20) = 40 m/s, not the simple mean.

hardQuiz.q: A runner completes 2.5 laps of a 400 m circular track, starting at the start line (she ends on the opposite side of the track). Her distance and the magnitude of her displacement are about:
hardQuiz.e: Distance = 2.5 × 400 = 1000 m. After a half lap she is at the opposite end of a diameter: d = C/π = 400/π ≈ 127 m.

hardQuiz.q: On a position–time graph, the curve rises, levels off, falls, levels off again, and then rises. While the curve is falling, the object is:
o: moving in the positive direction and slowing
accelerating at a constant positive rate
hardQuiz.e: A falling curve has a negative slope, so the velocity is negative: the object is moving back toward the origin. The level spots are where it stops and turns around.

hardQuiz.q: A 5.0 N force and a 7.0 N force act concurrently on a point. Which value could NOT be the magnitude of their resultant?
hardQuiz.e: The resultant must lie between |7.0 − 5.0| = 2.0 N and 7.0 + 5.0 = 12.0 N. 13 N is outside that range.

hardQuiz.q: A velocity vector of 25 m/s has a horizontal component of 20. m/s. Its vertical component is:

hardQuiz.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 8.0 m/s to 26 m/s while covering 102 m. What is its acceleration?

hardQuiz.e: Displacement is the trapezoid area: 0.5(4 + 14)(5) = 45 m.

hardQuiz.e: v0y = 30(0.60) = 18 m/s; time up = 1.8 s; total = 3.6 s.

hardQuiz.e: Average velocity = (20 + 0)/2 = 10 m/s; distance = 10 x 4.0 = 40 m.

hardQuiz.q: Two balls are released from the same height: one dropped, one thrown horizontally at 12 m/s. Which lands first?
o: They land at the same time
hardQuiz.e: Vertical motion is identical (same height, same g, zero initial vertical speed), so they land together.

hardQuiz.q: An object moving in the +x direction has a negative acceleration. It is:
hardQuiz.e: Velocity is positive and acceleration is negative (opposite signs), so the object slows down.

hardQuiz.e: $g = GM/R^2$; with M x2 and $R^2 x4, g$ is 2/4 = 1/2 of Earth's.

gravity provides the centripetal force that curves its path

a shorter period and faster speed
a longer period and faster speed

hardQuiz.q: A car horn emits 400 Hz. As the car speeds toward a stationary listener, the listener hears a frequency that is:
hardQuiz.e: Approaching source compresses wavefronts, raising the observed frequency.

hardQuiz.q: Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air. A person hears an echo from a cliff 1.0 s after shouting. The cliff is:
hardQuiz.e: Sound covers there and back: 340 m total, so the cliff is 170 m away.

hardQuiz.q: Two waves of equal amplitude A meet exactly out of phase. The resulting amplitude is:
hardQuiz.e: Completely destructive interference: the displacements cancel.

PART_C.sa:
Take the direction back toward the pitcher as positive.
(a) Impulse J = m(v_f - v_i) = 0.145(50 - (-40)) = 0.145(90) = 13.05 kg*m/s ~ 13 N*s.
(b) F_avg = J / t = 13.05 / 0.0080 = 1631 N ~ 1.6 x 10^3 N, directed back toward the pitcher.

(a) Find the speed at the bottom of the ramp. (b) Find how far it slides on the rough surface before stopping. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) Energy conservation on the ramp: mgh = 0.5 m v^2 -> v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 3.0) = sqrt(60) = 7.75 m/s.
(b) Friction force f = mu_k mg = 0.25(2.0)(10) = 5.0 N.
Work-energy theorem: f d = 0.5 m v^2 = 0.5(2.0)(60) = 60 J.
d = 60 / 5.0 = 12 m.

PART_C.q: A projectile is launched from ground level at 50 m/s at an angle of 37 degrees above the horizontal (sin37 = 0.60, cos37 = 0.80, g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Find the time of flight. (b) Find the horizontal range. (c) Find the maximum height. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
v0x = 50(0.80) = 40 m/s; v0y = 50(0.60) = 30 m/s.
(a) Time up = v0y/g = 30/10 = 3.0 s; total time of flight = 6.0 s.
(b) Range = v0x x t = 40 x 6.0 = 240 m.
(c) Max height = v0y^2/(2g) = 900/20 = 45 m.

PART_C.q: A 1500 kg car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 60 m at a speed of 18 m/s (g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Calculate the centripetal force required. (b) Calculate the minimum coefficient of friction between the tires and road that makes this possible. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) F_c = m v^2 / r = 1500(18^2)/60 = 1500(324)/60 = 8100 N, directed toward the center.
(b) Friction must supply F_c: mu_s(mg) >= F_c.
mu_s >= 8100 / (1500 x 10) = 8100 / 15000 = 0.54.
