(a) Elastic PE converts to KE: 0.5 k x^2 = 0.5 m v^2.
v = x sqrt(k/m) = 0.10 sqrt(800/0.50) = 0.10 sqrt(1600) = 0.10(40) = 4.0 m/s.
(b) KE converts to gravitational PE: 0.5 m v^2 = mgh.
h = v^2/(2g) = 16/20 = 0.80 m.

PART_C.q: A string 0.90 m long is fixed at both ends and supports a standing wave with 3 antinodes (the third harmonic). The wave speed on the string is 120 m/s. (a) Find the wavelength. (b) Find the frequency. (c) Find the fundamental frequency of this string. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) Third harmonic: L = 3(lambda/2) -> lambda = 2L/3 = 1.80/3 = 0.60 m.
(b) f_3 = v/lambda = 120/0.60 = 200 Hz.
(c) Fundamental f_1 = f_3 / 3 = 200/3 = 66.7 Hz (also f_1 = v/(2L) = 120/1.80 = 66.7 Hz).

PART_C.q: A 6.0 V battery is connected to a network: a 2.0 ohm resistor in series with a parallel combination of two 6.0 ohm resistors. (a) Find the equivalent resistance of the whole network. (b) Find the total current from the battery. (c) Find the voltage across the parallel section. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) Parallel pair: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so R_parallel = 3.0 ohms.
Total R = 2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0 ohms.
(b) I_total = V/R = 6.0/5.0 = 1.2 A.
(c) V across parallel = I x R_parallel = 1.2 x 3.0 = 3.6 V (the 2.0 ohm resistor drops the other 2.4 V).

PART_C.q: An electron (mass 9.1e-31 kg, charge 1.6e-19 C) moves at 2.0e6 m/s perpendicular to a uniform 0.0040 T magnetic field. (a) Calculate the magnetic force on the electron. (b) Calculate the radius of its circular path. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) F = qvB = (1.6e-19)(2.0e6)(0.0040) = 1.28e-15 N.
(b) The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: qvB = m v^2 / r.
r = m v / (q B) = (9.1e-31)(2.0e6) / ((1.6e-19)(0.0040)) = 1.82e-24 / 6.4e-22 = 2.8e-3 m (about 2.8 mm).

PART_C.q: A transformer steps 7200 V down to 240 V for household use. The primary coil has 3000 turns and the household load draws 30 A. Assume the transformer is ideal. (a) Find the number of turns on the secondary. (b) Find the current in the primary. (c) Explain why power companies transmit electricity at high voltage. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) N_s/N_p = V_s/V_p -> N_s = 3000(240/7200) = 3000/30 = 100 turns.
(b) Ideal: V_p I_p = V_s I_s -> I_p = (240 x 30)/7200 = 7200/7200 = 1.0 A.
(c) At high voltage the current is small, and resistive line losses are I^2 R, so lower current means far less energy wasted as heat in the transmission lines.

PART_C.q: Light travels from air (n = 1.00) into a block of glass (n = 1.50) with an angle of incidence of 40 degrees (sin40 = 0.643). (a) Find the angle of refraction in the glass. (b) Find the speed of light in the glass. (c) Find the critical angle for the glass-air boundary. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2): (1.00)(0.643) = (1.50) sin(theta2) -> sin(theta2) = 0.429 -> theta2 = 25.4 degrees.
(b) v = c/n = 3.0e8 / 1.50 = 2.0e8 m/s.
(c) sin(theta_c) = n_air/n_glass = 1.00/1.50 = 0.667 -> theta_c = 41.8 degrees.

PART_C.q: In a photoelectric experiment, light of wavelength 4.0e-7 m strikes a metal whose work function is 3.0e-19 J (h = 6.63e-34 J*s, c = 3.0e8 m/s). (a) Find the photon energy. (b) Find the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons. (c) State what happens if the light intensity is doubled. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) E = hc/lambda = (6.63e-34)(3.0e8)/(4.0e-7) = 1.989e-25 / 4.0e-7 = 4.97e-19 J.
(b) KE_max = E - W = 4.97e-19 - 3.0e-19 = 1.97e-19 J.
(c) Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons, so about twice as many electrons are ejected per second, but the maximum kinetic energy of each electron is unchanged (it depends only on frequency).

PART_C.q: A 0.30 kg mass on a spring (k = 120 N/m) is pulled 0.10 m from equilibrium on a frictionless surface and released. (a) Find the period of oscillation. (b) Find the total mechanical energy. (c) Find the maximum speed of the mass. Show all work.

A solid disk (I = 0.5 M R^2) of mass 4.0 kg and radius 0.25 m is initially at rest. A constant force of 12 N is applied tangent to its rim for 3.0 s. (a) Find the torque. (b) Find the angular acceleration. (c) Find the angular velocity after 3.0 s. Show all work.

A uranium-238 nucleus (92 protons, 146 neutrons) undergoes alpha decay, then the daughter undergoes beta-minus decay. (a) Give the atomic number and mass number of the nucleus after the alpha decay. (b) Give the atomic number and mass number after the subsequent beta-minus decay. (c) Explain what happens to a neutron in beta-minus decay.
PART_C.sa:
(a) Alpha decay removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons (mass number down 4): Z = 90, A = 234 (thorium-234).
(b) Beta-minus decay: a neutron becomes a proton, so Z increases by 1 and A is unchanged: Z = 91, A = 234 (protactinium-234).
(c) In beta-minus decay a neutron converts into a proton, emitting a high-speed electron (the beta particle) and an antineutrino; charge and nucleon number are conserved overall.

PART_C.q: A 1000 kg roller-coaster car starts from rest at the top of a 25 m hill. It descends a frictionless track and then enters a circular loop of radius 8.0 m (g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Find the speed of the car at the bottom of the hill. (b) Find the speed at the top of the loop (16 m above the ground). (c) Determine whether the car makes it around the loop.
PART_C.sa:
(a) Energy conservation: mgh = 0.5 m v^2 -> v = sqrt(2 x 10 x 25) = sqrt(500) = 22.4 m/s.
(b) At the top of the loop, height = 16 m: mg(25) = mg(16) + 0.5 m v_top^2.
v_top^2 = 2 x 10 x (25 - 16) = 180 -> v_top = 13.4 m/s.
(c) Minimum speed to maintain contact at the top: v_min = sqrt(g r) = sqrt(10 x 8.0) = sqrt(80) = 8.9 m/s. Since 13.4 m/s > 8.9 m/s, the car completes the loop.

PART_C.q: A 0.50 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s on a frictionless track collides with a stationary 1.5 kg cart. After the collision the 0.50 kg cart is at rest. (a) Find the velocity of the 1.5 kg cart after the collision. (b) Determine whether kinetic energy is conserved and classify the collision. Show all work.
PART_C.sa:
(a) Momentum: 0.50(3.0) + 1.5(0) = 0.50(0) + 1.5(v).
1.5 = 1.5 v -> v = 1.0 m/s.
(b) KE_before = 0.5(0.50)(9.0) = 2.25 J.
KE_after = 0.5(1.5)(1.0^2) = 0.75 J.
Kinetic energy is NOT conserved (2.25 J -> 0.75 J), so the collision is inelastic.

PART_C.q: A 25 ohm heating element is connected to a 120 V source. (a) Find the current through the element. (b) Find the power it dissipates. (c) Find the electrical energy it converts to heat in 10 minutes. Show all work.

A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 20 m/s brakes and skids to a stop. The coefficient of kinetic friction between tires and road is 0.80 (g = 10 m/s^2). (a) Find the friction force. (b) Find the deceleration. (c) Find the skid distance. Show all work.

A pendulum of length 2.5 m swings with a small amplitude (g = 9.8 m/s^2). (a) Find its period. (b) Find its frequency. (c) State two changes that would each double the period, or explain why one is not possible.
PART_C.sa:
(a) T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 2 pi sqrt(2.5/9.8) = 2 pi sqrt(0.255) = 2 pi (0.505) = 3.17 s.
(b) f = 1/T = 1/3.17 = 0.32 Hz.
(c) To double T you could make the length 4 times as large (T is proportional to sqrt(L)), or move to a location where g is one-fourth as large. Changing the bob's mass or the (small) amplitude would NOT change the period.

workedExamples.title: Adding perpendicular displacements
workedExamples.prompt: A student walks 30 m east, then 40 m north. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant displacement.
steps: The two legs are perpendicular, so use the Pythagorean theorem: R = √(30² + 40²) = √(900 + 1600) = √2500
Direction from tanθ = opposite/adjacent = 40/30, so θ = tan⁻¹(1.33) ≈ 53.1°, measured north of east

workedExamples.title: Percent error of a measurement
workedExamples.prompt: A lab group measures free-fall acceleration as 9.62 m/s². The accepted value is 9.80 m/s². What is their percent error?

workedExamples.title: Constant acceleration from rest
workedExamples.prompt: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 3.0 m/s² for 6.0 s. Find its final speed and the distance it covers.
steps: Known: vᵢ = 0, a = 3.0 m/s², t = 6.0 s
Final speed: v_f = vᵢ + at = 0 + (3.0)(6.0) = 18 m/s
Distance: Δx = vᵢt + ½at² = 0 + ½(3.0)(6.0)² = ½(3.0)(36) = 54 m

workedExamples.title: Ball rolling off a table
workedExamples.prompt: A ball rolls off a 1.25 m high table at 2.0 m/s horizontally. How long is it in the air, and how far from the table does it land? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
steps: Vertical motion is free fall from rest: 1.25 = ½(9.8)t²
Horizontal velocity stays 2.0 m/s: x = (2.0)(0.505) ≈ 1.01 m
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 0.51 s in the air, lands ≈ 1.0 m from the table

workedExamples.title: Pulling a box against friction
workedExamples.prompt: A 5.0 kg box is pulled across a floor by a 30 N horizontal force. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. Find the box's acceleration. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
steps: On a level floor the normal force equals the weight: N = mg = (5.0)(9.8) = 49 N
Kinetic friction: f = μₖN = (0.20)(49) = 9.8 N, opposing the motion
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 4.0 m/s² in the direction of the pull

workedExamples.title: Apparent weight in an elevator
workedExamples.prompt: A 60 kg student stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at 2.0 m/s². What does the scale read? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
steps: Forces on the student: normal force N up, weight mg down
Newton's second law with up as positive: N − mg = ma
The scale reads the normal force, which is more than the true weight of 588 N

workedExamples.title: Friction needed on a flat curve
workedExamples.prompt: A 1200 kg car rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m at 15 m/s. What centripetal force is needed, and what is the minimum coefficient of static friction? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
steps: On a flat road, static friction supplies this force: μₛmg ≥ mv²/r
workedExamples.answer: 5400 N; μₛ must be at least ≈ 0.46

workedExamples.title: Satellite in circular orbit
workedExamples.prompt: A 1000 kg satellite orbits Earth at r = 7.0 × 10⁶ m from Earth's center. Find the gravitational force on it and its orbital speed. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², M_Earth = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
steps: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r)

workedExamples.title: Torque on a wrench
workedExamples.prompt: A 40 N force is applied at the end of a 0.25 m wrench. Find the torque when the force is perpendicular to the wrench, and when it is at 60° to the wrench.
steps: τ = rF sinθ, where θ is the angle between the wrench and the force
Only the perpendicular component of the force turns the bolt

workedExamples.title: Balancing a seesaw
workedExamples.prompt: A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 40 kg child sit on the other side to balance it?
steps: Balance means zero net torque: clockwise torque = counterclockwise torque
The weights (mg) are perpendicular to the board, so τ = mg·d for each child

workedExamples.title: Cars that stick together
workedExamples.prompt: A 1500 kg car moving at 20 m/s hits a stationary 1000 kg car, and they lock together. Find their speed just after the collision and the kinetic energy lost.
steps: KE lost = 120,000 J (40% of the original), turned into heat, sound and deformation
workedExamples.answer: 12 m/s; 1.2 × 10⁵ J of kinetic energy lost

workedExamples.title: Speed on a frictionless track
workedExamples.prompt: A roller coaster starts from rest at the top of a 20 m hill. Ignoring friction, how fast is it moving when it is 5.0 m above the ground? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
steps: Mechanical energy is conserved: mgh₁ = mgh₂ + ½mv²; mass cancels

workedExamples.title: A series–parallel circuit
workedExamples.prompt: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω resistors. Find the total current and the current through each parallel resistor.
steps: Total resistance: 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 Ω; total current I = V/R = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A
Voltage across the 4.0 Ω resistor: (2.0)(4.0) = 8.0 V, leaving 4.0 V across the parallel pair
6.0 Ω branch: 4.0/6.0 ≈ 0.67 A; 3.0 Ω branch: 4.0/3.0 ≈ 1.33 A (they add to 2.0 A ✓)
workedExamples.answer: 2.0 A total; ≈ 0.67 A through 6.0 Ω and ≈ 1.33 A through 3.0 Ω

workedExamples.title: Force between two charges
workedExamples.prompt: Charges of +3.0 μC and −2.0 μC are 0.10 m apart. Find the magnitude and type of the force between them. (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
steps: Opposite signs, so the force is attractive

workedExamples.title: Proton in a magnetic field
workedExamples.prompt: A proton moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a 0.50 T magnetic field. Find the magnetic force on it and the radius of its circular path. (q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
steps: The force is always perpendicular to v, so it acts as the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r

workedExamples.title: Step-down transformer
workedExamples.prompt: An ideal transformer has 500 turns on its primary, connected to 120 V, and 25 turns on its secondary. Find the secondary voltage, and the primary current when the secondary delivers 2.0 A.
steps: An ideal transformer conserves power: V_pI_p = V_sI_s

workedExamples.title: Mass on a spring
workedExamples.prompt: A 0.50 kg mass on a spring with k = 200 N/m oscillates with an amplitude of 0.10 m. Find the period, the frequency and the maximum speed.
steps: Maximum speed at equilibrium: v_max = A√(k/m) = 0.10 × √400 = 0.10 × 20 = 2.0 m/s

workedExamples.title: Designing a 2-second pendulum
workedExamples.prompt: How long must a simple pendulum be to have a period of 2.0 s? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
steps: L ≈ 0.99 m, about one meter; the mass of the bob doesn't matter

workedExamples.title: Wavelength of a musical note
workedExamples.prompt: The note A4 has a frequency of 440 Hz. If sound travels at 343 m/s in air, what is its wavelength?
steps: Wave equation: v = fλ, so λ = v/f

workedExamples.title: Harmonics on a guitar string
workedExamples.prompt: A 0.65 m guitar string, fixed at both ends, carries waves at 260 m/s. Find its fundamental frequency and its third-harmonic frequency.
steps: For a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental has λ = 2L = 1.30 m
Harmonics are whole-number multiples: f₃ = 3f₁ = 600 Hz

workedExamples.title: Refraction into glass
workedExamples.prompt: Light in air hits a glass block (n = 1.50) at 40° from the normal. Find the angle of refraction and the speed of light in the glass. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
steps: Snell's law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂ → (1.00) sin 40° = 1.50 sinθ₂
sinθ₂ = 0.643/1.50 ≈ 0.429, so θ₂ ≈ 25°: the ray bends toward the normal

workedExamples.title: Image from a converging lens
workedExamples.prompt: An object is 30 cm in front of a converging lens with focal length 10 cm. Where is the image, and what are its size and orientation?
steps: d_i = 15 cm (positive: a real image on the far side of the lens)
Negative m means inverted; |m| = 0.5 means half the object's size
workedExamples.answer: Real image 15 cm behind the lens, inverted, half size

workedExamples.title: Photoelectric effect with green light
workedExamples.prompt: Light of wavelength 500 nm shines on a metal with a work function of 2.0 eV. Find the photon energy and the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

workedExamples.title: Radioactive half-life
workedExamples.prompt: A sample contains 80 g of an isotope with a half-life of 5.0 days. How much remains after 20 days?
steps: Each half-life halves the amount: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5.0 g
